What does Manton say about how a believer’s experience of God’s grace influences their desire for further communion with Him?

Manton teaches that tasting the Lord’s graciousness creates a yearning for more intimate fellowship. He explains that once a believer has "tasted that the Lord is gracious," this experience "kindles affection, and makes us long for more," leading to a renewed resolution to serve the Lord more faithfully and to walk in holiness. He further notes that "When you find benefit by one duty, it will be an encouragement to come again," indicating that each encounter with divine grace fuels a deeper desire for continued communion. [Manton — Works Vol14]

What does the sermon say about the responsibility of God's people in seeking the salvation of souls and the consequences of failing to do so?

Spurgeon teaches that believers are accountable for earnestly seeking the salvation of souls, warning that neglect brings severe accountability. He states, "if you who are His people are not earnest in seeking the salvation of souls, and they perish, their blood will be required at your hands!" The sermon underscores that while God’s sovereign will ultimately prevails, human earnestness in prayer and evangelism is essential; otherwise, the consequences fall upon the neglectful believers, as illustrated by the example of King Joash deciding whether the Syrians should be beaten three or six times. [Sermon 2303 — "Three Arrows--or Six?"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2303 — "Three Arrows--or Six?"]
meta.passage:
Things are often left to the will of men, yet everything does come to pass, in the end, according to the will of God! Can you not believe them both? And is not the space between them a very convenient place to kneel in, adoring and worshipping Him whom you cannot understand? If you could understand your religion, it would be one that did not come from God--it would have been made by a man of limited capacity, like yourselves, who was, therefore, able to make what you can comprehend. But inasmuch as there are mysteries in your faith, to the top of which you cannot climb, be thankful that you need not climb them.

But sometimes a practical question about these two points does arise. It is correct to say, speaking after the manner of men, "If men are earnest, if men are believing, if men are prayerful, such and such a blessing will come." And that the blessing does not come may be rightly traced to the fact that they were not as prayerful and as believing as they ought to have been. I believe that God will save His own elect, and I also believe that if I do not preach the Gospel, the blood of men will be laid at my door. I believe that God will give to His Son to see the travail of His soul, but yet, if you who are His people are not earnest in seeking the salvation of souls, and they perish, their blood will be required at your hands! This remark seems to be suggested by the story before us. God knew how many times the Syrians would be beaten and yet He left king Joash to decide whether they should be beaten three times or six times.

According to Gill, how does God's providence relate to natural and necessary actions?

Gill teaches that the providence of God is concerned in all actions, "from the beginning to the end of it," and that He is a "God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1 Sam. 2:3). He explains that every muscular motion—such as birds flying, fish swimming, and humans walking—is continued by God's providence, because all motion ultimately comes from the first Mover, "in whom we live, and move, and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Gill further distinguishes that necessary actions either arise from the necessity of nature or are appointed by God's ordination. This shows that both natural activities and those required by nature are under divine governance. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

What covenantal promise does Gill describe regarding believers being adopted as children of God?

Gill teaches that the covenant includes a promise that believers "should be openly adopted, and declared the children of God," meaning that God will treat them as His own offspring, granting them the status of His people, heirs, and portion. This adoption signifies a relational bond whereby God becomes their Father and they become His children, receiving both the discipline of the covenant rod and the inheritance promised to His people. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

According to Witsius in the Economy of the Covenants, how many appearances of God to Abraham are recorded?

Witsius states that the scriptural record shows that "the scriptures testify, that God appeared eight times to Abraham." He includes this detail as part of his brief overview of the appearances made to Abraham and the covenant that followed, emphasizing its role in the doctrine of grace from Abraham to Moses. According to the 1708 sermon, what are the three distinct ways the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers?

The sermon explains that the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers in a threefold manner. First, He is described as “the Holy Spirit was to be their Comforter, that they might not be afraid,” providing comfort and courage. Second, He serves as “their Advocate, that they might not be baffled,” defending and guiding them. Third, He operates as a divine power in communication: “When they spoke, there would be a power within them suggesting their words, a power with those words convincing their hearers, and a power in their hearers causing the word spoken to abide in their memories.” In this way the Spirit works within the speaker, persuades the listener, and secures the spoken word in memory. [Sermon 1708 — "The Holy Spirit's Threefold Conviction of Men"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1708 — "The Holy Spirit's Threefold Conviction of Men"]
meta.passage:
Never man spoke like that Man! Never did such wisdom and prudence dwell in any mind as dwelt in the mind of Christ! His Presence was their protection, the broad shield behind which they securely stood, whatever shafts might be shot at them by their adversaries. But now that He was to depart out of the world unto the Father, they would be deprived of their fortress and high tower--they would be as children bereft of their father, or, at best, as soldiers without a general. Here was a sad case. Work given and power with-drawn--a battle beginning and the conquering Captain leaving.

How happy it was for these disciples that our blessed Lord could tell them that His going away would be for their gain rather than for their loss! For when He was gone, the Spirit of God would come to be an Advocate for them and with them, and by His power they would be able to silence all their enemies and achieve their mission! The Holy Spirit was to be their Comforter, that they might not be afraid, and their Advocate, that they might not be baffled. When they spoke, there would be a power within them suggesting their words, a power with those words convincing their hearers, and a power in their hearers causing the word spoken to abide in their memories--that power would be Divine, the power of the Holy Spirit, who is One God with the Father and the Son.

It is one thing for men to speak, and quite another thing for God to speak through men.

Why does Manton argue that one must not delay the work of saving one's soul until later in life?

Manton teaches that a person must begin the work of salvation immediately because "death comes by way of surprise; it finds us before we look for it," and postponing it leads to grief when one is too weak to bear it. He warns that waiting until the appointed time "to think of saving our souls" is foolish, likening it to a traveller who sets out at night or the foolish virgins who bought oil too late. The urgency is rooted in the belief that we are sent into the world for "our trial and for our exercise," not for idle pleasure. [Manton — Works Vol16]

What are the threefold subordination of Christ that Hodge identifies in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 3:23‑63?

Hodge explains that “the Scriptures speak of a threefold subordination of Christ.” He outlines the three aspects as follows: (1) “A subordination as to the mode of subsistence and operation, of the second, to the first person in the Trinity,” which maintains the unity of substance while distinguishing roles; (2) “the voluntary subordination of the Son in his humbling himself to be found in fashion as a man, and becoming obedient unto death,” indicating Christ’s self‑limitation in incarnation; and (3) “the economical or official subjection of the theanthropos,” referring to Christ’s functional role in the redemptive administration. [Hodge — Commentary 1Corinthians]

What does the sermon warn about using encouragements to believe as a 'halfway house' before true faith?

Spurgeon warns that treating encouragements to believe as a provisional resting place is dangerous, stating that "If encouragements to believe are used as a sort of halfway house to rest in before actually believing, they are mischievously used and may ruin our souls!" He illustrates the peril by contrasting this with the example of the afflicted woman who, out of genuine confidence in Christ, pressed directly to the Savior’s garment and was healed. The sermon emphasizes that true faith, not mere encouragement, brings wholeness, and that after such healing a period of fear may follow as a natural response to the joy of salvation. [Sermon 3020 — "Good Cheer From Grace Received"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3020 — "Good Cheer From Grace Received"]
meta.passage:
If encouragements to believe are used as a sort of halfway house to rest in before actually believing, they are mischievously used and may ruin our souls!

This afflicted woman did not require to be cheered so soon, for she had such confidence in Christ and such a resolve to put her confidence to the test, that difficulties could not hinder her, nor crowds keep her back. The Savior was in the press--she joined the throng and with a holy boldness mixed with a sacred modesty she came behind Him, only wishing to touch His garment, or even the fringe of it--feeling persuaded that if she did but come into contact with the Lord, no matter how, she would be healed. According to her faith so was it done to her! And it was after she had been healed that our Lord spoke comfortingly to her He brought not forth the cup of cordial till the need for it had fully come. After she had touched Him and her faith had made her whole, a trial awaited her and her spirit was ready to faint--and then the tender One cheered her by saying, "Your faith has made you whole: go in peace."

It happens to many and many a heart that after it has obtained the blessing of salvation and has been healed of the disease of sin, a time of fear occurs. After it has made its confession of faith, a season of trembling follows occurring, perhaps, as a reaction from the joy of salvation, a rebound of the spirit from excessive delight.

According to the 1689 Second London Confession, what happened to Christ after his death and before His resurrection?

The 1689 Second London Confession teaches that after Christ’s crucifixion He "remained in the state of the dead, yet saw no corruption" and that "on the third day he arose from the dead with the same body in which he suffered". What does Spurgeon say about how God protects Christ’s fame against blasphemy and rebellion in Sermon 3436?

Spurgeon teaches that, although Christ is blasphemed by rebels, dishonored by apostates, and grieved by humanity, God will not allow His fame to be tarnished even for a moment. He emphasizes that God has declared, "He has glorified You," and that the Father has exalted the Son with a name above every name that will never be second. Moreover, Spurgeon declares that "God has glorified Him in the entire economy of salvation," ensuring that the crown remains safe upon Christ’s head despite the nations’ rebellion. [Sermon 3436 — "Christ Glorified"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3436 — "Christ Glorified"]

And though He is blasphemed by rebels, dishonored by apostates and grieved by ourselves, yet God, after all, shall not suffer Christ's fame to be tarnished for a single moment by all this, for He has said, "He has glorified You." I don't know that I can preach from the text, but I do know what I can do. I can feel thrice happy at the thoughts which it raises in my mind! It is so delightful to think that the crown is safe upon His head, though the nations rebel and the kings take counsel against Him, that his shield is forever glorified and untarnished, let men do what they may! Him has God the Father exalted and given Him a name which is above every name, which is first and chief and shall never be second, but shall forever reign and must reign till He has put all His enemies under His feet.

Now glancing across the subject, as some skiff flies over the sea, we will talk about what God has done by way of glorifying His Son, Jesus--

From first to last, Christ glorifies His Father, and the Father glorifies Him. Begin with that which has no beginning, namely, everlasting love, and we find that we are chosen in Christ Jesus from before the foundation of the world.

How does Manton explain the changing ways in which God is near to His people?

Manton teaches that God’s nearness is not constant in the same manner, but varies according to divine purpose and human experience. He writes that God is “nearer to us sometimes than at others, when we have more evidences of his favour inward or outward,” describing inward evidences as moments when He “quickens, comforts, supports the soul, filleth the heart with joy and peace in believing.” Conversely, he notes that outwardly “sometimes God hideth himself, some times seemeth not to mind the affairs of his people, at other times all the world shall know that they are near and dear to him.” Manton also affirms that while God “is not alike always present with his people, but never withdraweth that influence that is necessary to the being of grace,” He remains ever‑present in a sustaining way. This dynamic picture shows that God’s presence can be felt both in hidden and manifest forms, according to His good pleasure. [Manton — Works Vol09]

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 1064, how is merit treated in the doctrine of salvation?

Spurgeon teaches that merit has no place in the Christian Church and that all salvation is received solely by God’s free favor. He declares that “Merit is an unknown word in the Christian Church--it is banished once and for all” and emphasizes that every blessing comes through grace, not human achievement. Consequently, boasting is excluded because “not of works, lest any man should boast.” In this view the Apostle’s declaration, “By Grace are you saved, through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast,” underscores that salvation is a gift, not a merit‑based reward. [Sermon 1064 — "Salvation All of Grace"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1064 — "Salvation All of Grace"]
meta.passage:
Grace, all along, "reigns through righteousness unto eternal life," and, "where sin abounds, Grace does much more abound." There is no point in the history of a saved soul upon which you can put your finger and say, "In this instance he is saved by his own merit." Every single blessing which we receive from God comes to us by the channel of free favor, revealed to us in Christ Jesus our Lord. Boasting is excluded because merits are excluded. Merit is an unknown word in the Christian Church--it is banished once and for all--and our only shouts over foundation or top stone are, "Grace, Grace unto it!"

Perhaps the Apostle is the more earnest in insisting upon this Truth of God here, and in many other places, because this is a point against which the human heart raises the greatest objection. Every man, by nature, fights against salvation by Grace. Though we have nothing good in ourselves, we all think we have! Though we have all broken the Law and have lost all claim upon Divine regard, yet we are all proud enough to fancy that we are not quite so bad as others--that there are some mitigating circumstances in our offenses and that we can, in some measure, appeal to the justice as well as to the compassion of God.

Hence the Apostle puts it so strongly, "By Grace are you saved, through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast." The statement of the text means just this--that we all need saving--saving from our sins and saving from the consequences of them.

Why does Calvin describe Abraham as "the father of all them that believe" in his commentary on Galatians and Ephesians?

Calvin teaches that Abraham exemplifies the principle of justification by faith, showing that righteousness comes solely through belief and not works. He points out that Scripture declares "the same are the children of Abraham" and that there is "no variety of roads to righteousness," so Abraham serves as the universal pattern for all believers. Because God justified Abraham on the basis of his faith, Calvin concludes that Abraham is rightly called "the father of all them that believe," (Romans 4:11) and his example establishes the rule for obtaining righteousness for every nation. [Calvin — Commentary Galatians Ephesians]

What does Perkins’ Golden Chain say are the two parts of the sacramental word, and what roles do they play in a sacrament?

Perkins explains that the sacramentall word consists of two distinct elements: the commandment and the promise. He writes, "The sacramentall word, is the word of institution, the which God after a seuerall manner, hath set downe in each Sacrament." The commandment is the directive by which Christ appoints the administration of the sacrament and the receiving of it, as illustrated in Baptism (“Go into the whole world baptizing them in the Name…”) and the Lord’s Supper (“Take, eat, drink, doe ye this”). The promise, on the other hand, is the assurance that the ordained elements serve as instruments and seals of divine grace, exemplified by the baptismal formula “I baptize thee in the name of the father, of the sonne, and of the holy Ghost.” Thus, the commandment governs the outward act, while the promise secures the inward grace. [Perkins — Golden Chain]

What does Edwards say about the reliability of people’s hearts in attaining heaven?

Edwards teaches that many who profess confidence in their own salvation are in fact vulnerable to backsliding and cannot be relied upon to reach heaven, because "the hearts of men are very unsteady; they are not to be trusted." He warns that even those who seem engaged may lose grace when temptations arise, and that without true divine assistance they will be "soon discouraged" and fall into the "fiery billows of God's wrath." [Edwards — Sermons Worcester Vol8]

What does the sermon say is necessary to 'lay hold on eternal life' and how is this connected to 'fight the good fight of the faith'?

The sermon teaches that laying hold on eternal life is not a passive or dreamy pursuit; it requires the believer’s utmost energy, personal effort, and the Divine assistance that comes through faith. It stresses that one must "fight the good fight of the faith" by personally possessing the inward life and displaying its power in daily conduct, rather than relying on mere reasoning or scholarly arguments. In other words, the two commands—"fight the good fight of the faith" and "lay hold on eternal life"—are inseparably linked, demanding active, faith‑driven struggle to obtain and live out the divine life. [Sermon 1946 — "Eternal Life Within Present Grasp"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1946 — "Eternal Life Within Present Grasp"]
meta.passage:
When I say unto you, "Lay hold on eternal life," do not imagine that this is to be done in a dream, or accomplished without awakening your utmost energies, nor even then without that Divine assistance which only faith can receive.

As my text follows the command to "fight the good fight of the faith," it teaches us that the best way of contending for the faith is for ourselves, personally, to lay hold on eternal life. You cannot defend the faith by mere reasoning-- victory does not come through an array of arguments which have been, before, used by men of learning--you must, yourself, possess the inward life and exhibit the force and power of it in your daily conduct if you would be successful in the holy war. Men who forget the Divine Life soon cast away the Divine Truth. If the life is not in us, we may make what profession of orthodoxy we like, but we shall, in all probability, before long, turn aside like others, unto crooked ways. Well are the two commands joined together--"Fight the good fight of the faith, lay hold on eternal life." It reminds me of our Lord's words, "I am the way, the truth and the life."

My Brothers and Sisters, there is a higher and a better life than that which is known to the most of men. There is an animal life which all possess; there is a mental life which lifts us up above the beasts, but there is another life as much above the mental life as the mental life is above the mere animal life! The bulk of men are not aware of this and when they are told of it, they do not believe the statement.

What does Gurnall say about the insufficiency of moral uprightness that lacks the aim of God's glory?

Gurnall teaches that moral uprightness that is not directed toward the glory of God is merely a partial virtue and therefore falls short of true uprightness. He explains that a person may act faithfully toward an earthly master, yet "God never looked at, or thought of, in all this, and so all worth nothing, because God is left out of the story." The ultimate purpose, he asserts, is to do everything "to the glory of God," quoting 1 Cor. X. 31, "Whatever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Moreover, he cites Eph. vi. 7 that servants must "do their service as to God, not to man;" thus the chief end of any duty is the glorification of God, not merely human approval. [Gurnall — Christian In Complete Armour]

According to Owen, what are the consequences of omitting the first intention of the law and proceeding “per saltum” to the latter?

Owen argues that skipping the first intention of the law and moving “per saltum,” to the latter, turns a law that was “designed for the good of all men” into “the danger of all and ruin of many.” He explains that this practice “takes away all security of their goods and estates” from peaceable subjects, allowing “every evil man … to take the goods of other men into his own possession” while the owner remains unaware of the cause. Consequently, the legal right to one’s own property is transferred to another, who is then enabled by force to keep it, undermining the principal end of the law to secure each person’s possession of his goods until a lawful conviction. [Owen — Works Vol13]

What metaphors does Swinnock employ to illustrate how ungodly men deceive and prey upon Christians?

Swinnock depicts ungodly men as employing a series of deceptive images: they are "about me like Bees, with honey in their mouths and a sting in their tails"; they act "as Butchers, they claw the Ox about the ribs, that they may have the fairer blow at his head"; and he likens them to a pelican that "swalloweth shell‑fish, and warmeth them in her stomach, but it is to make them gape, that she may pick them out of the shels (where they are safe whilst they are shut) and devour them." By using these vivid analogies, Swinnock warns that such men appear sweet or harmless while secretly preparing to trap and devour believers. [Swinnock — Works 1665]

What is the first way Spurgeon says people should ‘Come and see’ according to Sermon 633?

Spurgeon teaches that the initial method of ‘Come and see’ is by observation. He urges believers to “give attention to the teaching of the Gospel, to weigh it and prove it.” If the message proves false it must be cast away, but if it is found worthy it should be held fast and never let go. [Sermon 633 — "Two Loving Invitations"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 633 — "Two Loving Invitations"]
meta.passage:
Investigation is courted upon every point--the Gospel stands at her door and says, "Come in here, come and see." You have this short sentence, "Come and see," as, first of all, an encouragement to enquirers. Many of you are like John's disciples. They had heard John preach and they believed his word and when they saw Christ, to whom John pointed, they followed Him. But not knowing Him, they followed Him with a question upon the tip of their tongues--"Master, where do You dwell?" He said, "Come and see." You also are anxious to know Christ. You have heard His Word preached by some of His witnesses and you want to know Him personally for yourselves. You have a pressing question to put tonight and Jesus encourages you to ask. No--to come and get your own answer with your own eyes. "Come," He says, "Come and see."

There are three ways, I think, by which persons are to, "Come and see." One is by observation. We ought to give attention to the teaching of the Gospel, to weigh it and prove it. If it is found false we are to cast it away with decision. But if it is found worthy of our attention we are to hold it fast and never let it go. Many persons are careless. They will consider the last new novel, or they have been clamoring to get the "Life of Julius Caesar," to see what the Emperor of the French can have to say upon that subject. But concerning Christ Crucified they have no curiosity. They frequent their place of worship without feeling enough interest in the affair to ask themselves why they go.

Why does the sermon say that many believers fail to recognize the Holy Spirit as a person?

The sermon teaches that the difficulty stems from habit and language: believers are so accustomed to speaking of the Holy Ghost’s influence and operations that they "have acquired the habit of regarding the Holy Ghost as an emanation flowing from the Father and the Son, but not as being actually a person himself." Consequently, they tend to view the Spirit as a mere emanation rather than a true subsistence, one person in the essence of the Godhead. [Sermon 4 — "The Personality of the Holy Ghost"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 4 — "The Personality of the Holy Ghost"]
meta.passage: First of all, we shall have some little instruction concerning the proper personality of the Holy Spirit. We are so much accustomed to talk about the influence of the Holy Ghost and his sacred operations and graces, that we are apt to forget that the Holy Spirit is truly and actually a person—that he is a subsistence—an existence; or, as we Trinitarians usually say, one person in the essence of the Godhead. I am afraid that, though we do not know it, we have acquired the habit of regarding the Holy Ghost as an emanation flowing from the Father and the Son, but not as being actually a person himself. I know it is not easy to carry about in our mind the idea of the Holy Spirit as a person. I can think of the Father as a person, because his acts are such as I can understand. I see him hang the world in ether; I behold him swaddling a new-born sea in bands of darkness; I know it is he who formed the drops of hail, who leadeth forth the stars by their hosts, and calleth them by their name; I can conceive of Him as a person, because I behold his operations. I can realize Jesus, the Son of Man, as a real person, because he is bone of my bone and flesh of my flesh. It takes no great stretch of my imagination to picture the babe in Bethlehem, or to behold the "Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief," of the king of martyrs, as he was persecuted in Pilate's hall, or nailed to the accursed tree for our sins.

Which New Testament scriptures does Dabney cite to illustrate the future renewal of the earth and humanity’s role in it?

Dabney points to several New Testament passages that portray the consummation of redemption in a renewed creation. He notes that Revelation 5:10 declares that believers will be made "kings and priests" and will reign on the earth, a privilege linked to their present expectant glory. He also cites 2 Peter 3:13, which promises that believers may "look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness," tying this hope to the prior renovation of the earth by fire. Additionally, Revelation 21:1‑2 is referenced, describing "a new heaven and a new earth" and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from God. In verse 3, a great voice announces, "Behold the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them," indicating the final consummation of the Covenant of Grace. Through these citations, Dabney emphasizes the immutability of God's purpose of grace and the glorious destiny of creation as humanity’s heritage. [Systematic — Dabney Systematic Theology]

What does Owen claim about the relative chronology of the Hebrew vowel points and the change of the Hebrew letters?

Owen argues that the vowel points could not have been invented before the alteration of the Hebrew letters, which occurred in the days of Ezra; therefore, the points must be the work of the post‑Talmudical Masoretes. He writes, "the invention of the points must be of a later date than the change of the letters, which was in the days of Ezra ; and so, consequently, be the work of the post‑Talmudical Masoretes." He also dismisses the opposing view as "most uncertain conjectures." [Owen — Works Vol16]

According to the Puritan Catechism, how many persons are there in the Godhead?

The catechism answers that “There are three persons in the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” and it affirms that these three are one God, sharing the same essence and being equal in power and glory. [Puritan Catechism Q.6 — "Puritan Catechism"]

meta.heading: [Puritan Catechism Q.6 — "Puritan Catechism"]

Q. How many persons are there in the Godhead?
A. There are three persons in the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one God, the same in essence, equal in power and glory [1].

What does the Second Helvetic Confession say about the purpose of the law and its relation to Christ’s fulfillment?

The Second Helvetic Confession teaches that the law served as a tutor to lead sinners to Christ, stating that "the law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith." It further explains that because human flesh is weak, no one can satisfy the law, so Christ himself fulfills and perfects it, communicating his righteousness to believers by faith. Consequently, the moral law is "abrogated; that is, it does not henceforth condemn us, neither work wrath in us; 'for we are under grace, and not under the law'" while still being respected and not rejected. [Reformed — Second Helvetic Confession]

meta.heading: [Reformed — Second Helvetic Confession]
meta.passage: But the Scripture (to wit, of the law) has concluded all under sin, that the promise by the faith of Jesus Christ should be given to them which believe' ( Gal. iii. 21, 22 ). 'Therefore, the law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith' ( ver. 24 ). For neither could there ever, neither at this day can any flesh satisfy the law of God, and fulfill it, by reason of the weakness in our flesh, 2239 2239 That is, any man, although he be regenerate. which remains and sticks fast in us, even to our last breath. For the apostle says again, 'That which the law could not perform, inasmuch as it was weak through the flesh, that did God perform, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh' ( Rom. viii. 3 ). Therefore, Christ is the perfecting of the law, and our fulfilling of it; who, as he took away the curse of the law, when he was made a curse for us ( Gal. iii. 13 ), so does he communicate unto us by faith his fulfilling thereof, and his righteousness and obedience are imputed unto us. 856 The law of God, 2240 2240 To wit, the moral law, comprehended in the Ten Commandments. therefore, is thus far abrogated; that is, it does not henceforth condemn us, neither work wrath in us; 'for we are under grace, and not under the law' ( Rom. vi. 14 ). Moreover, Christ did fulfill all the figures of the law; wherefore the shadow ceased when the body came, so that, in Christ, we have now all truth and fullness. Yet we do not therefore disdain or reject the law.

What does the Scots Confession of 1560 say about the nature and composition of the kirk?

The Scots Confession teaches that the kirk is not merely a human institution but a divinely appointed community: "a kirk: that is to say, a company and multitude of men chosen of God, who rightly worship and embrace him, by true faith in Christ Jesus." It describes the kirk as the universal (Catholic) body of the elect from all ages, nations, and tongues, united in communion with the Father and the Son through the Holy Spirit. The confession further emphasizes that the kirk is the "body and spouse of Christ Jesus" and that true life and eternal felicity are found only within this holy communion, rejecting any notion that mere equity or justice can secure salvation apart from Christ. [Reformed — Scots Confession 1560]

According to Baxter, what elements must a sermon possess to avoid being merely an 'image' or a 'well‑dressed carcass'?

Baxter teaches that a sermon must be both convincing and illuminated by the 'light of evidence' and the 'life of zeal' so that it can truly communicate the truth to listeners. He warns that a sermon that is merely well‑crafted in words but lacks these qualities is "but an image, or a well‑dressed carcase." Moreover, he stresses that preaching involves "a communion of souls, and a communication of somewhat from ours to theirs," requiring the preacher to pour the fullest light of understanding into the hearers' hearts and affections. By furnishing sermons with solid evidence and fervent zeal, the preacher can force the ungodly to see the truth unless they "wilfully shut their eyes." [Baxter — Reformed Pastor]

What promise does Spurgeon cite for believers regarding the truths of God that are currently unknown to them?

Spurgeon teaches that believers should acknowledge their limited understanding and trust that God will reveal hidden truths in due time. He points to the biblical assurance that, "What I do you know not now; but you shall know hereafter," indicating that the mysteries of divine grace are not for us to grasp fully now, but will be disclosed when the Lord wills. This promise encourages humility and reliance on God's future revelation rather than presuming to know all things. [Sermon 599 — "The Certainty And Freeness Of Divine Grace"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 599 — "The Certainty And Freeness Of Divine Grace"]
meta.passage:
You who love to hear the Gospel preached to sinners do not be afraid of the doctrines of Sovereign Grace! And you who love Sovereign Grace but cannot well hear doctrine too high for your taste, do not be afraid of the free invitations of the Gospel and the wide door which Jesus opens for needy sinners in many passages of Scripture!

Let us receive all Truth and let us be willing to learn every lesson which the Lord has written, remembering that if we cannot as yet reconcile Truths of God, there is the promise--"What I do you know not now; but you shall know hereafter." If we could know everything, we would be gods! Being mortals, some things must be unknown to us. Let us know our ignorance and despair of becoming infallible and thus we shall be in the path to true wisdom! But, if we boast of our wisdom, we shall be on the high road to great folly.

Let us consider the text carefully. And as it divides into two branches, let us view them one by one. Here we have Grace and Truth triumphant in specialty. And, secondly, we have Grace and Truth triumphant in liberality. May God help us to handle these so that much instruction may flow from them.

In the first sentence, we have GRACE TRIUMPHANT IN SPECIALTY--

"All that the Father gives Me shall come to Me." I would bring out the meaning of this passage by a few observations.

You perceive here that the Lord Jesus leads us up to the original position of all things--for since a people were given to Him by the Father, it is clear that they must first have been in the Father's hands.

What specific command does God give concerning His people in Sermon 221?

Spurgeon teaches that God’s concern for His people extends beyond their physical needs to their comfort, declaring, "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people." This command highlights that the Lord desires not only the preservation of His people but also their happiness and well‑being. [Sermon 221 — "Comfort Proclaimed"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 221 — "Comfort Proclaimed"]
meta.passage:
"My people!" O my hearers, can you by faith put yourselves in that number who believe that God says of them, "My people?" Can you look up to heaven to-night, and say, "My Lord, and my God: mine by that sweet relationship which entitles me to call thee Father; mine by that hallowed fellowship which I delight to hold with thee when thou art pleased to manifest thyself unto me as thou dost not unto the world?" Canst thou, beloved, put thine hand into thine heart and find there the indentures of thy salvation? Canst thou read thy title writ in precious blood? Canst thou by humble faith lay hold of Jesus's garments, and say, "My Christ?" If thou canst, then God saith of thee, "My people;" for if God be your God, and Christ your Christ, the Lord has a special, peculiar favour to you; you are the object of his choice, and you shall be accepted, at last, in his beloved Son. 

How careful God is of his people; those of whom he says, "My people;" mark, how anxious he is concerning them, not only for their life, but for their comfort. He does not say, "strengthen ye, strengthen ye my people;" he does not say to the angel, "protect my people;" he does not say to the heavens, "drop down manna to feed my people;"—all that and more also his tender regard secures to them; but on this occasion, to show us that he is not only regardful of our interests, but also of our superfluities, he says, "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people." He would not only have us his living people, his preserved people, but he would have us be his happy people too.

What examples does Flavel cite to demonstrate how providence answers the prayers of the saints?

Flavel illustrates providence by recounting several striking incidents: Dodd felt an irresistible urge to visit a neighbour and arrived just as the man was about to hang himself; Dr. Tate’s wife, fleeing the Irish rebellion, found a bottle of warm milk that kept her child from dying; and a destitute woman, while searching a chest for supplies, discovered a piece of gold that met her immediate needs until another provision was provided. He also points to the biblical miracle when “the sea divided itself, just upon Israel’s cry to Heaven, Exod. xiv.” These narratives, he argues, show that such events are not merely casual but occur “immediately upon… and consontantly to, the prayers of the saints,” confirming that God’s timing is exact and purposeful. Flavel concludes that these providential moments fulfill the scriptural promise, “In the mount of the Lord it shall be seen,” Gen. xxil. 14. [Flavel — Mystery Of Providence]

According to Sermon 1066, how does the preacher describe the relationship between the natural seasons and the church's harvest activity?

The preacher portrays the natural summer as a time of spiritual scarcity, stating that "the summer of Nature is the winter of the Church, and the earth's winter is our harvest." In this metaphor the season that brings growth to the earth is depicted as a period of inactivity for the church, while the earth’s winter—normally a time of dormancy—corresponds to the time of spiritual harvest. Thus the sermon suggests that the church’s greatest opportunity for harvest will come when the natural world is in its own winter. [Sermon 1066 — "A Call For Revival"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1066 — "A Call For Revival"]
meta.passage:
Reapers are busy everywhere except in the fields of our Divine Boaz. All fields are ripe but those of Bethlehem! All barns are filling but those of the Great Husbandman! Christ Jesus has scarcely a sheaf ingathered of late. We hear of very few results from the sacred sowing of the Word of God. Here and there the Church, like Ruth, gathers an ear--a very precious ear, it is true--for who shall estimate the value of a single soul? But we have no wave-sheaves as in the days of Pentecost, or, if we have them, they are few and far between. And as for the harvest home which we have so long expected, our eyes fail in looking for it in vain.

As a Church constituting a part of the Master's field, we have had, for years, one continued harvest but still never such an one as has satisfied our spirits, for our idea of our King is such that the largest increase to His Church would not content us--we should still feel that our Lord Jesus deserved far more! As He has not yet seen of the travail of His soul so as to be satisfied, so neither are we, His servants, content on His behalf, but we long, and cry, and pray for a larger harvest as His reward for the dread sowings in bloody sweat and streams of vital blood of Gethsemane and Golgotha!

The time when our Churches can operate extensively with the greatest convenience will soon be upon us. We do not usually look for any great things during the summer, when congregations are scattered at the seaside and workpeople are busy many hours in the day. The summer of Nature is the winter of the Church, and the earth's winter is our harvest.

What four points does Manton identify regarding the duty of thanksgiving to God in the preface?

Manton teaches that the preface outlines four distinct observations about thanksgiving: (1) "That it is a debt we owe to God to give thanks 'for his benefits.'" (2) In thanksgiving we should especially acknowledge His spiritual benefits. (3) We must give thanks not only for the spiritual benefits received by ourselves but also for those granted to others. (4) Thanksgiving for spiritual benefits, whether to ourselves or others, should include recognition of the increase of grace as well as its beginnings. [Manton — Works Vol17]

What course of action does the preacher recommend after a believer has prayed and committed a difficulty to God?

Spurgeon teaches that once a difficulty has been faithfully committed to God, the believer should cease lingering in prayer and move forward with confidence, saying, "Forward! Forward!" He emphasizes that this action is not rash but rests on the solid fact that "prayer does avail with God," and that the believer should "boldly march on" trusting that the obstacle will be removed. [Sermon 548 — "Forward! Forward! Forward!"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 548 — "Forward! Forward! Forward!"]
meta.passage:
But, on the other hand, after having sought God's help and having received it, she frequently laughs at the impossibility and cries, "It shall be done." and then, instead of betaking herself any longer to her knees, she boldly marches on, believing that the difficulty will vanish before her, that the crooked will be made straight and the rough places plain. We are not to be always praying over a difficulty. When we have fairly committed it to God, we are to act upon the assurance that He has heard us.

Nor will such an action be the fruit of rashness for it is a solid and substantial fact that prayer does avail with God. Beloved, it strikes me that the advice which the Lord gave to Moses was such as He has given to the preacher tonight-- and that the message which Moses delivered to the children of Israel is a very fit one for me to deliver to you. Short, prompt, soldier-like, here is the whole of it--"Forward! Forward!" If you have been sitting down or tempted to go back--"Forward!" We have long been praying, let us tonight, "go forward." The one subject we shall take up and try to deliver to different classes of characters, is, "Thus says the Lord, you children of Israel, Forward!"

First, we will contemplate THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL AS A FLOCK OF FUGITIVES. And in this light they give encouragement to trembling sinners flying from the curse of the Law and from the power of their sins. I think I see those poor Israelites crowding together, all alarmed and afraid, whispering to one another some such trembling words as these--"I saw them.

According to the 1828 sermon, what characterizes the lowest step of human speech about God's works?

Spurgeon teaches that the lowest rung of praise is marked by a crude, fear‑filled reaction to God's power, noting that at this level "Men shall speak of the might of Your terrible acts." This reflects a response that is more about awe of divine terror than a deeper appreciation of His glory, serving as the starting point for the ascent toward more enlightened worship. [Sermon 1828 — "How "The Unspeakable" is Spoken of"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1828 — "How "The Unspeakable" is Spoken of"]
meta.passage:
He foresees an endless line of praiseful hearts and utters this sure prophecy, "One generation shall praise Your works to another, and shall declare Your mighty acts." But, as if he would not and could not leave the blessed task to others, but must continue his own joyful hallelujahs, he cries, "I will speak of the glorious honor of Your majesty, and of Your wondrous works." Whatever happens, we must, each one, extol the Lord! Whether the world grows atheistic or devout, our duty and our joy are one and the same--we are still to magnify the Lord our God. We do not wish to avoid this profound pleasure; no, rather we would abound in it more and more!

All this leads up to a consideration of the various ways in which men speak of the Lord and His acts when their minds are moved in that direction. All see not the same points of His greatness, neither do they see with the same eyes, nor speak in the same spirit. It is ours, at this time, to review the various orders of mankind, and to observe how the revelation of God to them affects their minds and moves their tongues. There is an ascending scale in the four sentences of our text, as the poet-Prophet observes and records the ascending forms of human thought and speech.

We begin at the lowest step of the ladder. "Men shall speak of the might of Your terrible acts." We mingle with the multitude during a great occasion of national calamity, or upon the receipt of thrilling news from a foreign land--and we hear THE AWE-STRUCK TALK of the throng.

What does Owen argue about the need to consult Old Testament passages that testify to Christ’s deity and the sufficiency of a few scriptural proofs?

Owen observes that the apologist "professeth not to divine what places of the Old Testament, wherein the deity of Christ is evidently testified unto, are corrupted by the learned man" and refuses to examine the annotations that would support such a defense. Nevertheless, Owen contends that this reluctance is unnecessary because, in his view, "the word of God being all and every part of it of equal truth, that doctrine which is founded on five places of divine writ must by all Christians be acknowledged to be as irrefragably confirmed as a hundred express places would be conceived to confirm if". Thus, Owen maintains that even a limited number of clear Old Testament testimonies are sufficient to substantiate the doctrine of Christ’s deity without exhaustive scholarly inquiry. [Owen — Works Vol12]

What does Spurgeon mean when he calls God “the God of Bethel” in Sermon 1267?

Spurgeon teaches that the title “the God of Betel” identifies the same unchanging God who revealed Himself to Jacob at Bethel and who continues to extend the early mercies of salvation to every believer. He emphasizes that God “does not change” and therefore the mercies once shown to Jacob are still available to us, even when we are “unprepared for them.” By contrasting the mutable moon with the immutable Creator, Spurgeon shows that the God of Bethel is the “Immutable God” whose “years there is no end,” the firm foundation on which the soul can find true rest. [Sermon 1267 — "The God of Bethel"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1267 — "The God of Bethel"]
meta.passage:
"I am the God of Bethel." You remember, some of you, perhaps, the first time when pardoning love was revealed to you--when you were brought to see the love of God in the great atoning Sacrifice of Jesus Christ! Well, tonight, the Lord says to you, "I am the same God as you have ever found Me. I have not changed. I change not, therefore you sons of Jacob are not consumed, even as your father Jacob was not consumed, for I was, even to him, the same God."

Brothers and Sisters, what a mercy it is that we have an Immutable God! Everything else changes. Yon moon, which but a little while ago was full, you see now young and new again and soon she will fill her horns. Everything beneath her beams changes like herself. We are never at one stage and our circumstances are perpetually varying. But You, O God, are the same and of Your years there is no end. Your creatures are a sea, but You are the terra firma and when our soul comes to rest on You, Rock of Ages, then we know what stability means and, for the first time, we enjoy true rest.

Trust in the Lord forever and rest in the Lord alone, for He changes not. "I AM THE GOD OF BETHEL. Does not that mean, first, that our God is the God of our early mercies? As we have already said, Bethel was to Jacob the place of early mercy. Let us look back upon our early mercies. Did they not come to us, as they did to him, unsought and unexpected and when, perhaps, we were unprepared for them?

Why does Owen say Peter was grieved when he asked Christ “Lovest thou me?”

Owen explains that Peter’s grief arose because his sincere love for Christ was being repeatedly questioned. The Holy Ghost notes, "Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me?" This repeated questioning reveals Peter’s deep concern that his love might not be sufficient, and Owen uses it to illustrate how all human doubts are essentially “questionings of his love.” He further connects this to the broader pattern of doubting as a provocation to Christ’s love, as seen in Zacharias’s questioning and Jesus’ rebuke of the disciples, "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you?" [Owen — Works Vol08]

How does Gill describe the ability of each party in the covenant of grace and the nature of their relationship of equality and subordination?

Gill teaches that the contracting parties in the covenant of grace are each fully able to perform what they have promised: “the Father is able to make good all that he has promised in it,” the Son “had power to assume human nature into union with his divine Person, and to lay down his life in that nature… and was able to work out the salvation of his people,” and the Holy Spirit “is a Spirit of power and might, and so able to perform the part he took in this covenant.” Yet Gill also observes that “in covenants… there is an inequality and subordination; especially in covenants, in which there is service and work to be done on one side, and a reward to be given in consideration of it on the other.” Therefore, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equal in nature, perfections, and glory, they voluntarily enter a subordinate covenant relationship, which is why the Son calls the Father “Lord and his God.” [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

According to the Westminster Shorter Catechism, what is the misery of the estate into which man fell?

The Westminster Shorter Catechism teaches that the misery of that estate is that "All mankind by their fall lost communion with God, are under his wrath and curse, and so made liable to all the miseries of this life, to death itself, and to the pains of hell forever." This description emphasizes the total loss of fellowship with God, the exposure to divine wrath, and the consequent suffering and eternal condemnation that result from humanity's fallen condition. [Westminster — Westminster Shorter Catechism]

Wherein consists the sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell?
A. The sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell, consists in the guilt of Adam's first sin, the want of original righteousness, and the corruption of his whole nature, which is commonly called original sin; together with all actual transgressions which proceed from it.

Q. 19. What is the misery of that estate whereinto man fell?
A. All mankind by their fall lost communion with God, are under his wrath and curse, and so made liable to all the miseries of this life, to death itself, and to the pains of hell forever.

Q. 20. Did God leave all mankind to perish in the estate of sin and misery?
A. God, having out of his mere good pleasure, from all eternity, elected some to everlasting life, did enter into a covenant of grace to deliver them out of the estate of sin and misery, and to bring them into an estate of salvation by a Redeemer.

What does Spurgeon say about the relationship between a person’s heart‑longings and their future character or deeds?

Spurgeon teaches that the condition of the heart is decisive for spiritual life, noting that unbelievers are "a people that do err in their heart" while true seekers "seek Him with their whole heart." He further explains that heart‑longings function as a kind of prophecy about a person’s future, observing that "the longings of a man are a pretty sure index of what he will be." Though capacity alone does not guarantee achievement, the intensity and direction of one’s desires shape how talents are applied and opportunities seized, ultimately leading a man to become "what he intensely longs to be," especially when those desires are formed early in youth. [Sermon 1586 — "Holy Longings"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1586 — "Holy Longings"]
meta.passage:
So then, dear Hearers, your heart-longings may furnish you with helps for self-examination and I beg you to apply them, as things of the heart touch the root of the matter. Unbelievers are "a people that do err in their heart" and men truly find the Lord when they "seek Him with their whole heart"--so that the heart is all-important and its longings are among the surest marks of its condition.

Moreover, heart-longings are prophecies of what a man will be. It is not always capacity, if we could ascertain it, which will certify us as to what a man will do, for many men of large abilities achieve nothing for lack of inclination-- their talents lie hidden in the earth and, albeit they might have succeeded marvelously well in certain pursuits--they do nothing at all remarkable because they have no tendencies in that direction. An individual may have the means to relieve the poor and yet never perform a charitable act from lack of generosity. Or he may have great mental powers and yet never produce a line of useful literature because he is eaten up with idleness. But other things being equal, the longings of a man are a pretty sure index of what he will be--they cannot create capacity, but they develop it--they lead to the use of means for its increase and they make the mind keen to seize opportunities.

By some means or other a man usually becomes what he intensely longs to be, especially if those desires are formed in early youth while yet the world is all before him where to choose.

What does Charnock say about worship that is only outward and not from the heart?

Charnock warns that offering merely external worship amounts to a contempt of God's sovereignty. He observes that "we contemn God's dominion when we give him the service of the lip, the hand, the knee, and deny him that of the heart" and that such "devout figures of the face, and uncomely postures of the soul" reduce God to "an insignificant Lord, not worthy of any higher adorations from us than a senseless statue." In this view, true worship must present God with "the cream and quintessence of our souls" rather than a superficial, bodily service. [Charnock — Existence And Attributes Of God]

According to Spurgeon, how did Jesus choose to speak to His disciples and what attitude should believers adopt in their own speech?

Spurgeon teaches that the Savior deliberately used simple, homely language when encouraging His disciples, avoiding any pretentious or grandiose style. He observes that “There is nothing about the Savior's language which makes you say to yourself, \"What a grand speech! What a rhetorician! What an orator He is!\"” and warns that anyone who impresses listeners with lofty rhetoric is likely missing the true purpose of a loving heart. Instead, believers are urged to emulate Christ’s tenderness, to be comforters, and to speak plainly so that their words truly uplift and encourage the "tender little ones" in the faith. [Sermon 2005 — "The Hairs of Your Head Numbered"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2005 — "The Hairs of Your Head Numbered"]
meta.passage:
Fear you not, therefore, you are of more value than many sparrows."

Brethren, admire the tenderness of our Lord Jesus and imitate it. Let us try to be equally kind to our fellow-Christians. Let us never attempt to show off, or to make ourselves somebody, or to exhibit our strength of faith--for that will grieve the tender little ones and make them shrink into self-doubts. Let us consider their weakness and the help that we can render them, their sorrow and the comfort that we can afford them. Jesus was Himself a Comforter, or He could not have spoken of "another Comforter." And so let us be comforters in our measure, treading in His steps.

This reminds me, also, to say how very homely the Savior's talk became with His disciples in consequence of this desire to cheer their hearts. Why, He talks, I have often thought, just in the way in which anyone of us would have talked to our children when desirous to encourage them! There is nothing about the Savior's language which makes you say to yourself, "What a grand speech! What a rhetorician! What an orator He is!" If any man makes you say that of him, suspect that he is off the lines a little. He is forgetting the true object of a loving mind and is seeking to be a fine speaker and to impress people with the idea that he is saying something very wonderful and saying it very grandly.

The Savior quite ignores all idea of beautiful expression in just trying to bring forth His meaning in the plainest possible manner.

What does Owen say about the effect of the love of Christ on the saints’ perseverance and obedience?

Owen teaches that the love of Christ is the supreme motive for Christian duty, asserting that “For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead.” He argues that this love not only avoids any laxity in doctrine but also “stirs up, provokes, and draws out into action, every thing that is free, noble, ingenuous, filial, and of a heavenly descent, in the saints of God.” Moreover, Owen states that the doctrine “strengthens their faith in God and in Jesus Christ; which is the bottom of all acceptable obedience whatsoever,” making the love of Christ the foundation for all obedient living. What reason does Owen give for the slight defects in the arrangement of his treatise?

Owen attributes the imperfections to the work’s original form, noting that “Slight defects in the arrangement, the renewed discussion of a point after it had been quitted, and the disproportionate space accorded to some parts of the subject, are explained, perhaps, by the circumstance that the treatise was originally a series of discourses.” He therefore suggests that the structural flaws stem from the treatise having been compiled from separate sermons rather than a single, unified composition. According to Manton, why do the children of God make more of a promise than others?

Manton teaches that the children of God make more of a promise because they both “value the blessing promised, partly because they are satisfied by the assurance given by God's word,” which causes their souls to be “lifted up to the constant and earnest expectation of the blessing promised.” This double motivation—appreciation of the promised blessing and confidence in God's word—sets them apart from those who pass by such promises with a careless eye. [Manton — Works Vol07]

What does Shedd say about the relationship between the atonement and faith in saving a soul?

Shedd argues that the atonement, in God’s mind, is inseparable from the purpose to apply it to individuals, because “by the fact that atonement in and by itself, separate from faith, saves no soul.” He explains that Christ’s death would have been in vain if no one believed, and that only when the death is “confided in as an atonement” does it become God’s propitiation for sin, enabling justification. Thus, faith is essential for the atonement’s saving effect. [Systematic — Shedd Dogmatic Theology Vol2]

Why does Owen claim that there will be no satiety or weariness in the eternal contemplation of God's glory?

Owen argues that the absence of satiety or weariness in heaven is due to the endless, ever‑new communications of the divine nature that flow through Christ. He explains that "there neither is, nor can be any satiety or weariness in heaven, in the eternal contemplation of the Grad glory" because the infinite fullness of God is continually poured into believers, providing perpetual fresh experiences that can never be exhausted. This perpetual influx of divine communication ensures that the heavenly vision remains perpetually new and never becomes stale. [Owen — Glory Of Christ]

How does Burroughs explain that worship draws believers nearer to the presence of God?

Burroughs teaches that worship is the primary means by which believers are drawn into the special presence of God. He explains that "the duties of his Worship are those means that the Lord hath appointed for the letting out of himself in the glory of his goodness and mercy to his people," and that through these duties believers experience the communication of God that makes His presence more special. Moreover, worship requires believers to "stir up the faculties of your souls, and all the graces of the Spirit of God," acting those graces upon God, which further brings them into close fellowship with Him. [Burroughs — Gospel Worship]

What does Flavel say a loss or breaking of patience under adversity reveals about a person's soul?

Flavel teaches that the loss or breaking of patience under adversity "argues a decay of strength in the soul" and warns that "If thou faint in the day " of adversity, thy strength is small." He explains that patience is a divine power to bear hard and heavy things according to God's will, distinguishing it from mere moral virtue. [Flavel — Works Vol01]

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 2353, how does he describe the condition of a soul that feels overwhelmed by sin?

Spurgeon teaches that a soul in such distress is "A SOUL BESET" and he illustrates this with the vivid lament, "For innumerable evils have compassed me about: my iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of my head." He reminds listeners that many true saints have walked this rough path before, urging that no troubled heart should fall into despair because others have endured the same painful experience. [Sermon 2353 — "Out Of The Depths"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2353 — "Out Of The Depths"]
meta.passage:
Others have been here before you! Others who were undoubtedly the people of God, others who were saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation!

You have had to write bitter things against yourself--so have other people. Have you ever felt as though you were surrounded by sin so that you could not look up? You are not the first man who has been in such a plight and you are not likely to be the last. This part of the road has been frequented by full many of the pilgrims bound to Zion's city. All the people of God have not taken this route--there are different ways of traveling along the road to Heaven. But some of the true saints of God have gone by this rough path and I mention this fact in order that no troubled heart may fall into despair because of the painful experience through which it is passing at the present time.

In trying to describe a soul in the condition mentioned in our text, let me say, first, that we have evidently before us A SOUL BESET--"For innumerable evils have compassed me about: my iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of my head."

The text describes a man who is, first, made to see the countless number of his sins. He did not know so much about them, before. He said that he was a sinner and he meant it, but then he wrote the words in very small letters.

According to the sermon, how does God regard sin and what is the means of its healing?

The sermon teaches that God, in His boundless compassion, regards sin not merely as a moral failing but as a disease that requires cure. It states that "GOD, IN INFINITE MERCY, HERE TREATS SIN AS A DISEASE" and that "By His stripes"—the suffering of the Lord Jesus—"we are healed." Thus, through Christ’s atoning wounds, believers receive the remedial grace that restores them from the deadly malady of sin. [Sermon 2000 — "Number Two-thousand--Healing by the Stripes of Jesus"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2000 — "Number Two-thousand--Healing by the Stripes of Jesus"]
meta.passage:
I said to myself, "That text will suit me well and, perhaps, a voice from God may speak through it, yet again, to some other awakened sinner." May He, who by these words spoke to the chamberlain of the Ethiopian queen who, also, was impressed with them while in the act of searching the Scripture, speak, also, to many who shall hear or read this sermon! Let us pray that it may be so! God is very gracious and He will hear our prayers.

The object of my discourse is very simple. I would come to the text and I would come at you! May the Holy Spirit give me power to do both to the glory of God!

In endeavoring to come to the full meaning of the text, I should remark, first, that GOD, IN INFINITE MERCY, HERE TREATS SIN AS A DISEASE. "By His stripes"--that is, the stripes of the Lord Jesus--"we are healed." Through the sufferings of our Lord, sin is pardoned and we are delivered from the power of evil--this is regarded as the healing of a deadly malady. The Lord, in this present life, treats sin as a disease. If He were to treat it once, as sin, and summon us to His bar to answer for it, we would, at once, sink beyond the reach of hope, for we could not answer His accusations, nor defend ourselves from His justice. In great mercy He looks upon us with pity and, for the time being, treats our ill manners as if they were diseases to be cured rather than rebellions to be punished. It is most gracious on His part to do so, for while sin is a disease, it is a great deal more!

If our iniquities were the result of an unavoidable sickness, we might claim pity rather than censure.

Why does Shedd claim that miracles are necessary and natural in the New Testament?

Shedd teaches that miracles belong to the super‑natural whole of the Redeemer’s person and work of redemption, so when the incarnation and resurrection are affirmed, miracles become both necessary and natural. He explains that “Old Testament miracles are connected with the Jehovah‑Angel, or the redeeming God. Those of the New Testament are connected with the Jehovah‑Logos, or Jesus Christ.” Consequently, anyone who believes that God incarnate has come to save humanity will readily accept the miracles, while disbelief in the divine‑human person who is “set for the fall and rising again of many” leads to rejection of them. [Systematic — Shedd Dogmatic Theology Vol1]

Whitaker argues that Luther did not introduce any novel doctrine but rather sought to revive the earlier tradition, stating that "Luther taught no new doctrine, he restored and mainteined the auncient Catholicke faith." According to Boyce's abstract, did the divine nature of Christ suffer during the incarnation?

Boyce argues that Scripture does not teach that the divine nature suffered; it teaches that the suffering belongs to the human nature of the second person of the Trinity, who became man. He notes that while the two natures are united in one person, the divine properties remain unchanged, and any suffering is ascribed only to the human nature. As he puts it, "the Scripture statements do not teach that the divine nature suffered." [Systematic — Boyce Abstract Of Systematic Theology]

It is alleged, that God cannot be without change, because He 
suffered during the incarnation of Christ. 

The argument is that the declarations about Christ's suffering 
are made, not simply of the human nature, but of both natures com- 
bined, and that thus we are taught, that it was not merely man, but 
God also that suffered. This position is assumed by some, who main- 
tain that Christ had a complete human, as well as divine nature, 
not a mere human body, but also a rational soul. It is neces- 
sarily also the position of those, who claim that He had no human 
soul, but that His divine nature took the place of a rational soul. 

The reply to this argument is that the Scripture statements do not 
teach that the divine nature suffered. This is nowhere said. They 
teach that the second person of the Trinity, who became man, suffered. 
But they plainly refer that suffering to His human nature only. They 
teach us, that in the relations of His natures to His person, He pre- 
served unchanged the properties and qualities, which belonged to 
them separately, and that this was especially true of the divine na- 
ture. There were indeed some communications from the divine 
nature to the human, but none from the human to the divine. But 
while thus distinct, they were united together in a single personality 
and by such a union, that whatever might be said, to be true or to 
be done, or to be suffered by either of the natures, might in like man- 
ner be affirmed of the person in whom they were united.

Why does Owen say that some people despise the preaching of the word and remain unreceptive?

Owen argues that the rejection of the gospel is not merely a matter of human preference but a divine judgment: many are "cast out of his care, — barren land ; he will till them no more" and are therefore given over to their own hearts' lusts. He explains that these multitudes are "rejected of God" and that the power of the Spirit is withheld from them, so the word "affects them no more." This spiritual abandonment results in a state where they "think none so happy as themselves" and despise those who love the waters of the sanctuary, making them incapable of expelling the gospel or quenching its light. [Owen — Works Vol09]

What does Manton say about the sin of idleness and the proper use of human labor?

Manton teaches that idleness is a grave sin because it harms both nature and the Spirit of God. He writes that "idle men quench the vigour of nature, and therefore are incapable of the quickenings of grace," and he links it to biblical condemnation, noting that "' Pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness,' were the sins of Sodom, Ezek. xvi. 49." According to Manton, every person has a divinely appointed function: "Every member of the body hath its function and use, whereby it becometh serviceable to the whole." Thus, to spend one’s life merely in eating, drinking, and sport is "beastly or brutish," and true purpose lies in diligent employment that furthers the public good and advances one toward heaven. [Manton — Works Vol19]

According to the sermon, how does Spurgeon illustrate the need for immediate obedience to Christ using the example of Zacchaeus?

Spurgeon teaches that believers must respond to Christ with the same urgency that Zacchaeus displayed, noting that when the Master said, "Make haste," Zacchaeus "made haste and came down." He warns that any delay, like the procrastination of Felix, is a dangerous spirit that can lead to perdition, and he exhorts the hearers to hear His voice without hesitation. The sermon stresses that immediate, obedient reception of Christ brings the "good of the land" and secures Christ as our Rock, Refuge, and Hiding Place. [Sermon 3487 — "The Honored Guest"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3487 — "The Honored Guest"]
meta.passage:
"He made haste and came down." It is not always easy to come down from a tree with great speed. He came down, however, as fast as he could. There was no hesitancy in his manner. I daresay his heart was down before his feet! In like manner they who would receive Christ must receive Him now. This is not a call or a counsel to be trifled with. The procrastination of Felix, which led him to say, "When I have a more convenient season I will send for You," is a very dangerous spirit. Let those who talked as Felix talked beware lest they perish as Felix perished! "Today, if you will hear His voice, harden not your hearts." Zaccheus made haste. They who receive Christ heartily must receive Christ immediately!

We notice, too, that Zaccheus received the Lord obediently. When the Master said, "Make haste," he made haste. Hardly had He said, "Come down," when down he came. If you, my Hearers, be likewise willing and obedient, you shall eat of the good of the land. Christ likes us to be obedient to Him, though He speaks to us less as a Lawgiver than as a Savior and a Friend. If we refuse to take His yoke upon us and learn of Him, how can we reasonably expect to find rest unto our souls? The words of Jesus must be deeply respected and diligently observed by those who would have Him for their Rock, their Refuge and their Hiding Place.

What purpose does the sermon say believers' trials and training serve?

Spurgeon teaches that the hardships believers endure are intentional preparation for service to others. He explains that "You are being led along a rough road and being tried and instructed in order that you may be the means of helping others" and that "You are being trained as a hardy mountaineer in order that when the Lord's sheep are lost on wild craggy places, you may know how to climb up after them and bring them down to a place of safety." This training equips Christians to rescue those lost in despondency and doubt, even though the full impact of one’s life on others may remain unknown until the end. [Sermon 2930 — "Hiding in You!"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2930 — "Hiding in You!"]
meta.passage:
You are being led along a rough road and being tried and instructed in order that you may be the means of helping others whom you will find in some of the dark places of the earth. You are being trained as a hardy mountaineer in order that when the Lord's sheep are lost on wild craggy places, you may know how to climb up after them and bring them down to a place of safety. You are being taught how to find your way through the country of despondency and despair in order that when the pilgrims to the Celestial City lose their way and get into the marshy places of fear and doubt, you may know how to bring them out again and set their feet again upon the Rock and establish their goings once more.

The bearing of any one man's life upon the lives of other men can scarcely be fully known to us here. Even when we are able to look upon the completed life, we shall hardly know how much it has been intertwisted with other men's lives and, certainly, until the life is completed, no man can know how much his present sufferings have to do with his usefulness to others. Nor can he fully understand how he is being prepared here, there, and in a thousand other places for usefulness in a position of which he little dreams that he will ever be the occupant. Yet he is one day to be placed where all this mysterious training will be of the utmost service to other people.

What does Hodge say the 'mystery of Christ' includes beyond the Gentiles being fellow‑citizens of the saints?

Hodge explains that the phrase "the mystery of Christ," which includes far more than the truth that the Gentiles were fellow‑citizens of the saints, refers to a broader divine purpose. He notes that "God by revelation had made known to Paul a mystery, or purpose, which was not revealed as it now was to the apostles," meaning that the Gentiles were to share in the blessings of the Messiah’s reign and be united as one body with the Jews in his kingdom, a plan foretold by the ancient prophets and now fully disclosed in the Gospel. [Hodge — Commentary Ephesians]

What does Owen say about the effect of godly sorrow on the believer’s prayer life?

Owen teaches that godly sorrow is a source of spiritual refreshment in prayer, writing that "There is great spiritual refreshment in that godly sorrow which is at work in our prayers." He explains that the Holy Ghost causes mourning, which paradoxically contains joy, and that this mourning leads to a "secret encouragement" to adhere constantly to God, even when believers lack a tangible sense of complacency. Thus, according to Owen, experiencing godly sorrow indicates that the Spirit is active and that the believer’s soul is being refreshed and drawn toward a holy rest in God. [Owen — Works Vol07]

What does Edwards say about the influence of natural and animal elements on a true Christian’s affections toward God?

Edwards observes that a Christian’s affections are not formed solely by holy and divine impulses, but are blended with natural and even animal forces. He notes that “the great mixture of that which is natural with that which is spiritual” is evident in the way divine influences manifest in certain families and individuals. Moreover, he warns that “in what true Christians feel of affections towards God, all is not always purely holy and divine; every thing that is felt in the affections does not arise from spiritual principles, but common and natural principles have a very great hand.” Thus, natural passions, self‑love, and bodily influences can shape and sometimes distort the spiritual affections that ought to be directed toward God. [Edwards — Distinguishing Marks]

What three differences of persons does Perkins identify for the proper distribution of alms?

Perkins teaches that almsgiving must be ordered according to three distinctions of people. He first states, "The first, is a mans owne: And such are they, that be of his houshold, for which he that makes not provision, is worse then an Infidell, as the Apostle speaketh, 1. Tim. 5. 8." This refers to one's own household and blood relatives, whose support is a primary duty. He then adds, "A second difference of men is this. Some are of the houshold of faith," indicating that members of the Christian community should be given preference after one's own family. Finally, he notes, "A third difference. Some are our owne poore, of our towne, land, & country: & some be strangers in the same respects," meaning that local poor and neighbors are to be considered before strangers. These three categories guide the conscience in charitable giving. [Perkins — Cases Of Conscience]
