What does Sermon 884 say about the pursuit of happiness through sin?

Spurgeon teaches that chasing happiness by sinful means only drives it farther away. He writes, "The more intensely you pursue happiness in the bewitching way of sin, the further will it fly from you." The sermon warns that such pursuit leads to danger, weariness, and a shipwreck of the soul, and that true peace is found only in a covenant with God. [Sermon 884 — "Help for Seekers of the Light"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 884 — "Help for Seekers of the Light"]
meta.passage:
The more intensely you pursue happiness in the bewitching way of sin, the further will it fly from you. Like the will-'o-the-wisp, the glare of pleasure will entice you into the quagmire and there will leave you to find that your chase has gained you nothing but danger and weariness. The pearl of happiness lies not in the depths of dissipation. The broad road always ends in destruction, never in peace.

Hoist the sails of desire to the breeze, let go the helm of reason and let your soul be borne wherever the blasts of temptation or the currents of custom may direct and one thing you may be sure of--your unhappy boat will never be drifted by such means into the haven of peace! To such a voyage shipwreck is the certain end! To other modes of living disappointment is in like manner attached. Vain is it to pile up gold. Vain is it to awaken the clarion trumpet of fame. Vain is it to gather learning or to master eloquence, eminence, rank, wealth, power--all these things are too little to satisfy the insatiable craving of an immortal soul.

You must have God or you shall never have enough! You must be reconciled to Him or you can never be at peace with yourself. Man must enter into a covenant of peace with his God or all the creatures of God shall conspire against him! Pilgrim of earth, your way must be towards holiness and God, or in vain shall you expect the dawning--to the sinner there is reserved the blackness of darkness forever and even now his way is hard and his path is darkened with fear and disquietude.

Who does Owen identify as the legitimate governors that could determine the liberty of Jewish Christians, and how does he distinguish them from false apostles?

Owen argues that the only legitimate governors who could make such a determination were the apostles themselves, noting that the decision was “a doctrinal declaration of the mind of the Holy Ghost” rather than an act of church power. He contrasts these lawful governors with the “false apostles” who “were none of their lawful governors, but went about as seducers, drawing away the disciples of the apostles from them.” [Owen — Works Vol15]

What does Owen claim about the king’s role in granting indulgences and its relation to the peace of the kingdom?

Owen argues that the monarch is uniquely qualified to decide whether an indulgence serves the nation’s stability, stating that the king is "the best and most competent judge of what will contribute to the peace of the kingdom" and that his royal intentions are guided by a clear understanding of their consistency with the kingdom’s welfare. He further expresses confidence that the king’s declarations have not been undermined and that a peaceful conduct by the subjects will aid the king’s successful governance. [Owen — Works Vol13]

What does Burroughs identify as the primary cause that leads the poor and discontented to become witches?

Burroughs teaches that the root of witchcraft is personal discontent. He explains that the Devil "fishes in troubled waters" and targets those whose spirits are "vexed" and "discontent at home," especially the poor, old, and melancholy. According to Burroughs, "the ground of all those that have been witches" is this inner dissatisfaction, which the Devil exploits by "fastens his temptations"—promising money to the poor or vengeance to the angry—thereby drawing them into unlawful courses. [Burroughs — Rare Jewel Of Christian Contentment]

Why does Reynolds say an aged man needs spectacles to read small print in the Treatise of the Passions?

Reynolds teaches that the aged man's difficulty in reading small print stems from a double defect: his bodily power is weakened and the letters lack sufficient materiality for his limited understanding. He illustrates this with the familiar similitude, stating that "an Aged man is not able to read a small Print, with out the Assistance of Spectacles to make the Letters by a refraction seeme greater." Thus the uncertainty of opinion arises from both the insufficiency of the understanding and the disproportion of the object to that understanding. [Reynolds — Treatise Of The Passions]

meta.heading: [Reynolds — Treatise Of The Passions]

Even so also the Ob jects of mans Vnderstanding must participate of the two contr
 •…
 ries, Abstraction and Materi ality. Abstraction first, in proportion to the
 
 of the Vnderstanding, which is Spi rituall. And Materiality too, in respect of the Sense, on which the Vnderstanding de pends in this estate, as on the Medium of Conveyance, and that is Corporall. So that where ever there is Difficulty and Vncertain ty of Operation in the Vnderstanding, there is a double defect and disproportion: first in the Power, whose Operations are restrained and limited for the most, by the Body: and then in the Object, which hath not a suffici ent mixture of those two qualities, which should proportion it to the Power. This is plaine by a familiar similitude; an Aged man is not able to read a small Print, with out the Assistance of Spectacles to make the Letters by a refraction seeme greater. Where first wee may descry an Imperfection in the Organ; for if his Eyes were as cleare

and well-dispos'd as a young mans, hee would be able by his Naturall Power, without Art, to receive the Species of small Letters. And next, there is an Imperfection and deficiencie in the Letters; for if they had the same Mag nitude and fitnesse in themselves, which they seeme to have by Refraction through the Glasse, the weaknesse of his power might haply have sufficient strength to receive them without those Helps. So that alwayes the Uncertainty of Opinion is grounded on the In sufficiencie of the Vnderstanding to receive an Object, and on the Disproportion of the Object to the Nature of the Vnderstanding.

What does Binning say about the proper way believers should regard the redemption they receive through Christ?

Binning teaches that believers ought to regard redemption not merely as a duty or task but as a privilege and dignity granted by Christ. He urges that one should "look upon it as the one half, and greater half of the benefite conferred by Christs death" rather than seeing it only as a requirement, because this perspective encourages gratitude and a deeper sense of the sufficiency of Christ’s work. By viewing redemption as a gracious gift, the believer is led to groan for the full redemption of both soul and body, seeking complete freedom from the law of sin. [Binning — Sinners Sanctuary]

Why does the sermon advise believers not to judge themselves by outward circumstances?

The sermon teaches that believers must not judge themselves by outward circumstances, because such signs are not the divine measure of worth. It states that “for these are not the balances of the sanctuary and cannot help you to a just conclusion as to your state before God!” Thus, external conditions do not determine a person’s standing before God, and affliction may be a sign of divine chastening rather than rejection. [Sermon 1671 — "The Value and Rank of the Believer"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1671 — "The Value and Rank of the Believer"]
meta.passage:
Many of those whom the Lord loves most, endure sharp affliction, even as the most precious metal is likely to see the most of the fire. Is it not written, "As many as I love I rebuke and chasten"? "What son is there whom his father chastens not?" The Lord scourges every son whom He receives. Therefore, never judge yourselves by outward circumstances, for these are not the balances of the sanctuary and cannot help you to a just conclusion as to your state before God! Everything may seem to go against you and yet all things may be working together for your good. Jacob was no good judge of his own matters when he cried, "All these things are against me!" He needed Egypt and a sight of Joseph to teach him the reason for the Lord's dealings.

Everything may be prospering with you openly and yet you may only be as the victim which is covered with garlands when it is being led to be slain at the altar. Everything may be grieving you and yet securing your best prosperity. Our Heavenly Father has, I think, given us the words of the text and the context by way of comfort in reference to His outward dispensations. If God has a favored people whom He has chosen--upon whom His distinguishing Grace has lighted to make them great and honorable--you would suppose that the second verse of this chapter would run thus, "You shall not go through the waters, for I will be with you to keep you out of them; neither shall you pass through the rivers, for I have bridged them on your behalf. You shall never go through the fire and, therefore, you shall not be burned.

According to the sermon, what consequence does Moses warn of for those who refuse to aid their fellow tribes in conquering the promised land?

Spurgeon teaches that Moses warned the Israelites that failure to assist their brethren would constitute a grave offense. He declared that "if they did not keep their covenant and give all due aid to their brethren, then they would sin against God and they might be sure that their sin would find them out," indicating that such neglect would be a sin against God that could not remain hidden. [Sermon 1916 — "The Great Sin Of Doing Nothing"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1916 — "The Great Sin Of Doing Nothing"]
meta.passage:
He, therefore, proposed to them that if they were to have that conquered country for their own, they should at least cross the river with their brethren and fight and continue fighting until the land on the other side of the Jordan had been cleared of its old inhabitants and the whole of Israel could take the whole of the country--and each tribe could possess its portion.

He put it to them as a matter of honor and as a matter of right, that they ought to help in conquering the rest of the land. Why should they receive their lot without fighting and leave the other tribes to bear the toil and danger of war? Had not God bid them all to go up and drive out the condemned Canaanites? How could they evade their duty without great sin? He would have them take their full share in the war and on that condition they might have the rich meadows of Bashan, but not otherwise. This was clearly just and equitable and commended itself to those concerned. They at once agreed to the proposal and Moses, to enforce the agreement, told them in the words of the text, that if they did not keep their covenant and give all due aid to their brethren, then they would sin against God and they might be sure that their sin would find them out.

I remarked, in reading the chapter, that Moses spoke very wisely, very forcibly, very honestly--and the people were very pliant. They yielded to his persuasions and the difficulty which threatened to divide the nation was readily remedied. It is well to have a wise leader.

According to Flavel, what is the reason believers should be satisfied with their material circumstances and how does faith relate to receiving the benefits of Christ?

Flavel teaches that believers are to be content with their outward lot because the true feast is spiritual, not material. He declares, "He suffered his flesh to be rent, and his blood set abroach for you : What love like the love of Christ !" and urges that, while the world offers "dainties" and "flesh of lambs and calves," the believer’s soul is nourished by the "flesh of Christ" and the "blood of Christ" through faith. He stresses that "the necessity of faith" is what allows a soul to "eat his flesh, and drink his blood," and that it is the "application of him by faith" that gives the sweetness and benefit of Christ, not any external preparation. Thus, contentment in material poverty is rooted in the surpassing spiritual nourishment received by faith. [Flavel — Works Vol06]

How does Spurgeon in Sermon 146 explain the proper way to assess a man's happiness?

Spurgeon teaches that true assessment of a man's happiness must include both his earthly life and his eternal destiny. He cites the heathen Solon, noting that "Call no man happy until he is dead; for you know not what changes may pass upon him in life." Accordingly, Spurgeon adds that a man's condition should be measured "from the coffin to the resurrection, and from the resurrection on throughout eternity." He also affirms the paradox that "To die is gain," emphasizing that ultimate happiness is found in the immortal state beyond death. [Sermon 146 — "The Good Man's Life and Death"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 146 — "The Good Man's Life and Death"]
meta.passage:
Stars die mayhap; it is said that conflagrations have been seen far off in the distant ether, and astronomers have marked the funerals of worlds, the decay of those mighty orbs that we had imagined set for ever in sockets of silver to glisten as the lamps of eternity. But blessed be God, there is one place where death is not life's brother, where life reigns alone; "to live," is not the first syllable which is to be followed by the next, "to die." There is a land where deathknells are never tolled, where winding-sheets are never woven, where graves are never digged. Blest land beyond the skies! To reach it we must die. But if after death we obtain a glorious immortality, our text is indeed true: "To die is gain."

If you would get a fair estimate of the happiness of any man you must judge him in these two closely connected things, his life and his death. The heathen Solon said, "Call no man happy until he is dead; for you know not what changes may pass upon him in life." We add to that—Call no man happy until he is dead; because the life that is to come, if that be miserable, shall far outweigh the highest life of happiness that hath been enjoyed on earth. To estimate a man's condition we must take it in all its length. We must not measure that one thread which reacheth from the cradle to the coffin. We must go further; we must go from the coffin to the resurrection, and from the resurrection on throughout eternity. To know whether acts are profitable, I must not estimate their effects on me for the hour in which I live, but for the eternity in which I am to exist.

What does Downame identify as the second cause that leads people to go on in sin without repentance?

Downame teaches that the second cause of security in sin is a lack of consideration: even when people know the danger, they neglect to reflect on it and cast it behind them, making no use of what they know. He writes, "The second cause of securitie is, when as knowing these things, for want of consideration we cast them negligently behind our backs, and make no vse of that we know." This negligence causes them to ignore the ever‑watching eye of the Judge and the future judgment, so they continue sinning without repentance. [Downame — Guide To Godliness]

According to Hodge, which sacraments do Roman Catholics regard as absolutely necessary for attaining salvation?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholics distinguish between absolute necessity and merely helpful means, and they hold that certain sacraments are absolutely necessary. He writes, "Baptism they hold to be absolutely necessary, either its actual reception, or the honest purpose to receive it, alike for infants and adults, as the sole means of attaining salvation." In the same vein, Hodge notes that they also consider Penance and Holy Orders absolutely necessary in the same sense, while other rites such as Confirmation, the Eucharist, Extreme Unction, and Marriage are viewed as necessary only because they are commanded or highly beneficial. [Systematic — Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology]

According to Gill, how is God's holiness compatible with the presence of sin in the world?

Gill teaches that God's holiness is displayed in his providential works, even when those works are dark and intricate, and that there is no criminal or sinful aspect in them. He emphasizes that the chief objection to God's holiness is the fact that sin exists, but asserts that God is "neither the author nor abettor of it; he neither commands it, nor approves of it, nor persuades to it, nor tempts nor forces to it." Rather, God forbids, disapproves, and chastises sin, yet overrules it for great good and His own glory, as seen in examples such as the fall of Adam and the crucifixion of Christ. Thus, the holiness of Jehovah the Father is observed in acts of grace, including the choosing of some in Christ to everlasting life before the world began. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

Why does Calvin insist on defending his doctrine even when he is accused of heresy?

Calvin argues that a minister cannot remain silent when his teaching is challenged, because silence would show a lack of regard for the public good. He states that "the defence of a good cause is not to be neglected," and emphasizes that ministers are appointed "to be as firm in defending as faithful in delivering it." Thus, he feels obligated to protect sound doctrine taken from the pure word of God. [Calvin — Tracts Vol3]

What does Spurgeon say about the purpose and divine design of the ocean in Sermon 1259?

Spurgeon teaches that the ocean is a providential provision of God, essential to the world much as blood is to the body, because it supplies navigation, abundant fish, and a health‑promoting freshness for mankind. He emphasizes that its perfect balance reveals "an amazing instance of Divine Wisdom" and that "In the ocean there is not a drop of water too much nor a drop too little!" This precise proportion, he argues, prevents disorder and sustains life, showing that God "has made nothing in vain." [Sermon 1259 — "There Go The Ships"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1259 — "There Go The Ships"]
meta.passage:
Remorselessly swallowing up all that is cast upon it, the thankless ocean makes no return of fruit or flower. Is not the larger part of the world given up to waste? "No," says David, and so say we--"There go the ships." The sea benefits man by occasioning navigation and yielding, besides, an enormous harvest of fishes of many kinds. Besides which, as the blood is necessary for the body, so it is necessary for this world that there should be upon its surface a vast mass of water in perpetual motion. That measureless gathering together of the waters is an amazing instance of Divine Wisdom in its existence, its perpetual ebb and flow and even in its form and quantity. In the ocean there is not a drop of water too much nor a drop too little! There is not a single mile of sea more than there ought to be, nor less than there should be.

An exact balance and proportion is maintained and we little know how the blooming of the tiny flower or the flourishing of the majestic cedar would be affected were the balance disturbed. Between the tiny drop of dew upon each blade of grass and the boundless main there is a relation and proportion such as only an infinite mind could have arranged. Remember, also, that the ocean's freshness tends to promote life and health among the sons of men. It is good that there is sea, or the land might devour its inhabitants by sickness. God has made nothing in vain. Ignorance gazes on the stormy deep and judges it to be a vast disorder, the mother of confusion and the nurse of storms.

What does Boyce say about the basis of the assurance that is not part of saving faith?

Boyce teaches that the assurance which is not a part of saving faith is an advanced stage of Christian experience and is grounded not on the objective truth of God’s word or Christ’s salvation but on the inner work of the Spirit. He states that this assurance “but that assurance would rest not on God's word, nor on Christ's salvation, but on the evidence afforded by the Spirits work in our hearts.” Consequently, it is a subjective confidence derived from the Spirit’s activity in the believer’s heart rather than from the external proclamation of the gospel. [Systematic — Boyce Abstract Of Systematic Theology]

What does Spurgeon assert about the authority of the Gospel in Sermon 2804?

Spurgeon teaches that the Gospel is presented to humanity as a command, possessing the authority that obliges obedience. He emphasizes that one cannot speak of obeying anything that lacks the authority of a command, and therefore the Gospel must be understood as having the force of a command. As he observes, "they have not all obeyedthe Gospel." [Sermon 2804 — "Disobedience to the Gospel"]

It is true of many who meet with us, in this House of Prayer, as it is of those who assemble elsewhere, that though they have often heard the Gospel, yet "they have not all obeyed the Gospel." How does Spurgeon describe the willingness of modern churches to readmit a repentant brother compared to the early church at Corinth?

Spurgeon teaches that modern churches should be far more willing to restore a penitent member than the early church at Corinth, noting that "I scarcely know a Christian church that would refuse to receive into its membership again, a brother who had erred if he showed signs of true repentance." He adds that the early churches also had faults and that today’s churches must avoid "unfair comparisons" and instead focus on personal sanctification to help improve the whole body of believers. [Sermon 2918 — "Facing the Wind"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2918 — "Facing the Wind"]
meta.passage:
I trust there is no Christian church, at least in our own denomination, that would endure such a thing for an hour! And when this man had been put out by Paul's command and proved penitent, then the Church at Corinth, which was a church that did not believe in ministry, you know, (there is a class of Christians of that sort, now, which resembles greatly these Corinthians), because they had once put him out, refused to receive him again though he was penitent and wanted to return.

I scarcely know a Christian church that would refuse to receive into its membership again, a brother who had erred if he showed signs of true repentance. The churches of today, compared with the early churches of Christ, can say that the Grace of God has been extended to us, even as unto them--and we now have no right to be continually crying down the operations of the Holy Spirit in the churches by making unfair comparisons between them and the churches of old. They had their faults, as we have ours. They came short in many respects, even as we do. Instead of bringing a railing accusation against churches as they are, the best thing is for everyone of us to do his best in the sight of God to make them what they should be, by seeking our own personal sanctification and endeavoring that the influence of a holy life shall, in our case, help to leaven the rest of the mass.

What does the Greenham work say about the relationship between prayer, faith, and knowledge?

The Greenham work teaches that prayer cannot be proper without both faith and knowledge, insisting that "must pray in faith, and he that will pray in faith, must also pray in knowledge." It further explains that believers should engage in frequent reading, hearing, and meditating on the word, because "For often reading, hearing, and meditating, bring ripenes of iudgement; often praying, applying, and examining our selues, bring quicknes of our affections." By coupling disciplined study with heartfelt prayer, the work argues that the Lord will supply grace and occasions for glory, enabling prayer that is both judged and affectively quick. How does Sibbes explain the presence of lingering sin after a person has received pardon?

Sibbes teaches that even after pardon the root of sin may still linger like the dregs of a disease, because sanctification proceeds gradually and each prayer and renewal of repentance carries away some of the debt until the final physician—death—perfectly cures both soul and body. He affirms that this does not indicate weak grace, but divine wisdom, concluding that "God is wise. Let us not quarrel with our physician, for he is wiser than we ourselves." [Sibbes — Works Vol02]

Why does the sermon claim that David's Psalms are especially appealing to seasoned believers?

Spurgeon teaches that David’s continual experience of severe trials gave him a unique insight into the human heart, allowing his Psalms to express both ecstasy and depression with precision. He writes, "Now, it is from this cause, I take it, that David's Psalms are so universally the delight of experienced Christians," because they mirror the full spectrum of emotional states that mature Christians have encountered. [Sermon 467 — "Flesh And Spirit--A Riddle"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 467 — "Flesh And Spirit--A Riddle"]
meta.passage:
He had temptations from within, for the man after God's own heart not only knew what it was to be assailed, but to be carried by storm, by fierce and terrible passions. I may grant, perhaps, that Job's trial was more severe than any that fell to David. But yet I know not. Possibly the burning of Ziklag--when his wives were carried away captive, and all that he had was consumed, and his men spoke of stoning him--may have been even a severer trial than Job's when he sat upon a dunghill and scraped himself with a potsherd.

And I am not sure, but I think that mournful procession over the brook Kedron in David's later life, when his own son thirsted for his blood, had in it a Gethsemane bitterness that is hardly to be found in the tribulation which fell to the Patriarch of Uz. Job must fairly yield the palm in one respect, for his was no life-long siege but only one sharp and furious attack. David, however, no sooner escaped from one trial, than he fell into another. He no sooner emerged from one season of despondency and alarm, than he was again brought into the lowest depths and all God's waves and billows rolled over him.

Now, it is from this cause, I take it, that David's Psalms are so universally the delight of experienced Christians. Into whatever frame of mind we may be cast, David seems to have described our emotions, whether they ARE of ecstasy or depression, to the very letter. He was an able master of the human heart, because he had been tutored in that best of all schools, the school of real, heartfelt, personal experience.

What reason does Edwards give for why fore‑known events must actually exist, based on God's immutable knowledge?

Edwards argues that because God's knowledge is immutable, it cannot change or be succeeded by a new view; therefore any event that God foreknows cannot fail to exist. He explains that "the immutability of knowledge makes his knowledge to be without succession" and concludes that "it is utterly impossible the known events should fail of existence." Since a failure would require a change in God's knowledge, which is impossible, the existence of fore‑known events is guaranteed. [Edwards — Freedom Of The Will]

How does the sermon describe the effect of emphasizing free grace on a preacher’s attitude toward sin?

Sermon 1416 teaches that the advocate of free grace is "most plain and severe in denouncing sin with all his might and most tender in sorrowing over his own personal iniquities." This shows that the emphasis on free grace produces a preacher who both condemns sin strongly and mourns it deeply. [Sermon 1416 — "The Faithful Saying"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1416 — "The Faithful Saying"]
meta.passage:
The union of these two feelings in Paul is, by no means, an unusual occurrence among human minds, for you will generally find that the preacher who is most clear in his witness that salvation is by Grace, is also the man to whom sin is exceedingly sinful! Indeed, all those who prize Grace most are men who feel most sorrow concerning their transgressions.

All systems of theology, except that which is founded upon Free Grace, in some way or other take off the edge of guilt. If they try to compromise the business and make salvation to be partly a matter of human effort and human merit--and partly a work of Divine Grace--they are sure, in the process, to conceal the exceeding iniquity of sin. Man is made out to be a poor, weak creature victimized by a Law too rigid for his frailty. It is represented that he has a right to mercy and a great uproar is made if we deny him any such right! And much anger is felt if we declare that mercy is the Sovereign prerogative of God which may be exercised at His own absolute discretion.

Rebellion against Divine Election is often founded on the idea that the sinner has a sort of right to be saved and this is to deny the full guilt of sin. You will find that he who sets forth Free Grace as the only fountain and source of human salvation--and declares that sin is pardoned and put away freely by the mercy of God in Christ Jesus--is most plain and severe in denouncing sin with all his might and most tender in sorrowing over his own personal iniquities.

What twofold classification of keeping God's commandments does Manton give in Works Vol09, and how does he characterize the legal keeping?

Manton explains that there is "a twofold keeping or doing of the commandments — legal and evangelical." He describes the legal keeping as the exact obedience required by the rigor of the law, saying it is "when we do them so exactly as is answerable to the rigour of the law, and the rule of strict justice doth require, which exactness is when our obedience is universal in every point, when everything commanded by God is done by us without failing in one point." What does Calvin say is present in the Lord's Supper, and how does the Reformed view of the mode of reception differ from the Lutheran view?

Calvin teaches that the presence in the Lord's Supper is not the natural body and blood of Christ but "a supernatural, life-giving influence emanating from his glorified body in heaven, and conveyed to the believer by the power of the Holy Ghost." The Reformed position holds that the mode of reception is spiritual, with "the organ is not the mouth, but faith," and the condition of reception is the presence and exercise of faith, contrasting with the Lutheran view that the body and blood are received "corporaliter" through the mouth and actual consumption of the elements. [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol3]

How does Manton describe the relationship between delight in God's statutes and the ability to remember His word?

Manton teaches that spiritual affections are strengthened through disciplined practice and that delight in God's statutes safeguards memory. He writes, "Meditation breedeth delight, and delight helpeth memory and practice." By taking pleasure in the statutes, the mind is drawn to what the heart loves, preventing forgetfulness: "Delight preventeth forgetfulness; the mind will run upon that which the heart is delighted in;" Thus, remembering God’s word becomes a source of contentment rather than a burden. What does the sermon say about Jesus' attitude toward being called “a friend of publicans and sinners”?

The sermon observes that Jesus repeated the title himself and was not at all embarrassed by it, even seeming to enjoy it as a distinction. It notes that He “takes the title home to Himself and wore it as some distinction which He was glad to have,” and that He “says it and He takes care to say it again and to bid both Matthew and Luke record it.” Thus, according to the sermon, Jesus was unashamed of the label and embraced it in a higher, better sense than his contemporaries understood. Yet people are often so indifferent about their soul affairs that the littlest trifle in a service, the tiniest accidental thing will often keep them from listening to the most weighty Truths of God that concern their immortal interests!

Now let us come to this title of our Master. They called Him, "a friend of publicans and sinners." It is somewhat noticeable that He quotes this saying Himself. Probably neither Matthew, nor Mark, nor Luke, nor John would have told us that they called Jesus, "a friend of publicans and sinners" if He had not repeated it, Himself. It is clear from this fact that He was not in the least ashamed of the title! He repeats it almost as if He enjoyed it, as if He took the title home to Himself and wore it as some distinction which He was glad to have! He, Himself, says it and He takes care to say it again and to bid both Matthew and Luke record it, that He was called, "a friend of publicans and sinners." What He was not ashamed to repeat, we are not ashamed to think of at this service! So, first of all, let us notice that this saying, in the sense in which they meant it, was not true. But, secondly, in a higher and better sense than they understood it, it was true.

What eight supports does Brooks provide for believers who have lost assurance?

Brooks outlines eight biblical supports for those who have lost assurance. The first is that “the great God might have burnt up all, he might not have left one house standing.” The second support is "That God has given them their lives for a prey." The third points to the common lot of sinners and saints. The fourth declares that even though believers have lost much as citizens, merchants, and tradesmen, they have lost nothing as “Cliristians, as they are saints, as they are the called of God.” The fifth assures that the Lord will certainly make up all their losses. The sixth promises that by fiery dispensations the Lord will make way for the new heavens and the new earth and the glorious deliverance of his people. The seventh foretells that God will bring about the ruin and destruction of his and his people's enemies. The eighth concludes that all shall end well and all shall work for good. [Brooks — Complete Works Vol6]

According to Sibbes in Works Vol03, what is the manner in which the Holy Spirit guides believers?

Sibbes teaches that the Holy Spirit, sent by the Father and Christ, does not direct believers instantly but gradually forms a habit in them that disposes them toward good. This reflects the descent of grace and wisdom from Christ to the Spirit to believers, enabling them to walk wisely, graciously, in the Spirit, and in Christ as one. [Sibbes — Works Vol03]

What does Ambrose say is the purpose of Christ’s ascension and sitting at the right hand of God?

Ambrose teaches that Christ’s ascent was not an end in itself but a preparation for the work of dispensing divine blessings to the saints. He explains that after rising, “Christ is gone up to heaven, Christ is set down at God's right hand,” where He is “invested with all the riches of Heaven” and holds “all the keyes of Heaven and Hell.” From that position He “gave gifts unto men, yea, he gave the gift of gifts, even the Holy Ghost himself,” so that believers may partake of that Spirit. Thus the purpose of the ascension is to enable Christ to bestow the Holy Spirit and all heavenly riches upon His people. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

What three elements does Witsius say the apostle proposes in his discourse, and how does he interpret the phrase “before the world began” concerning election?

Witsius teaches that the apostle’s discourse presents three things in order: first, “the purpose of God, which is the spring of all grace”; second, the promise made from the remotest antiquity; and third, the actual showing and manifestation by the glorious coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Concerning election, Witsius argues that the expression “before the world began” in its full emphasis signifies eternity, and therefore provides a strong argument for the eternity of election. [Systematic — Witsius Economy Of The Covenants Vol2]

What does Spurgeon say about the way the Holy Spirit brings light into a man's soul in Sermon 1252?

Spurgeon teaches that the Holy Spirit initiates the work of creation in man by mysteriously entering the soul and brooding over it, and as the first blessing the Lord sends light into the heart. He explains that this light is conveyed through the Word of God, the Logos, which pours life and illumination into humanity. The apostle’s light reveals both the man's guilt and the way of salvation, showing the Person and work of Christ and making redemption obtainable by simple belief. As Spurgeon notes, the Lord God declares, "Let there be light," and the Spirit, through the Word, fulfills that promise. [Sermon 1252 — "The First Day Of Creation"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1252 — "The First Day Of Creation"]
meta.passage:
The Lord begins His work upon man by the visitation of the Spirit, who enters the soul mysteriously and broods over it, even as of old He moved upon the face of the waters. He is the Quickener of the dead soul. In connection with the Presence of the Holy Spirit, the Lord sends into the soul, as His first blessing, light. The Lord appeals to man's understanding and enlightens it by the Gospel. The heavenly light reveals to man his obligations to God and his forgetfulness of them. It shows him the evil of sin, his own guilt, consequent danger and the impossibility of his escaping from that danger by any efforts of his own.

That same light, also, reveals to man God's way of salvation--shows him the Person of Christ, His work, its suitability and its freeness--and lets him see how he may obtain an interest in redemption by the simple act of believing. It is a blessed thing for any man when the Lord God says concerning him, "Let there be light." If you keep your eyes upon the chapter you will observe that the light came into the world at first by the word--"God said, 'let there be light.'" It is through the Word of God contained in this book, the Bible, that light comes into the soul. Let me correct myself--it is by Him who is called the Logos, THE WORD, that light is poured into the heart of man, for, "in Him was life, and the life was the light of men."

This is that true light which lights every man that comes into the world. The Spirit, you see, is engaged in the new creation--He broods over the soul.

What reason does Downame give for God requiring outward service in addition to inward piety?

Downame teaches that God does not rest solely on inward devotion, but "the Lord doth chiefly require and delight in the inward seruice of the soule, and the integrity and since rity of the heart; yet doth he not rest in it alone, but requi reth also the seruice of the body and outward man," so that the hidden righteousness of the heart may be manifested to others. By expressing inner holiness through outward conduct, believers become "declared righteous before them" and thus receive visible justification before men as well as the inward justification by faith before God. [Downame — Guide To Godliness]

Why does Ambrose claim that seeking earthly comforts is ultimately futile?

Ambrose teaches that the pursuit of earthly comforts is futile because the earth is a place of sorrow, trouble, and mourning rather than lasting pleasure. He asks, "Oh why do we seek the living among the dead?" to illustrate the emptiness of seeking life in a world destined for death, and he contrasts the fleeting joys of the wicked with the eternal reward promised to the godly. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

How does Sermon 2806 illustrate the woman's continual acknowledgment of Jesus as Lord?

Spurgeon teaches that the woman’s confession of Jesus as Lord persists through every stage of His ministry and suffering. She perceives Him as “a friend of publicans and sinners,” knows Him as the “Lord of the sea who made the stormy waves lie still at His command,” and even at the crucifixion she still salutates Him as Lord, echoing the dying thief’s prayer, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom." This unbroken recognition demonstrates her belief that He is the Son of the Highest despite His humiliation. [Sermon 2806 — "Jesus Our Lord"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2806 — "Jesus Our Lord"]
meta.passage: She sees that He is a friend of publicans and sinners, yet she believes Him to be the Son of the Highest, though flesh and blood have not revealed that great Truth of God to her. Even in His humiliation, she knows Him as Lord of the sea who made the stormy waves lie still at His command, and as the Master of diseases, before whom all manner of sicknesses, and even devils, themselves, fled apace. She knows Him to have been a suffering Man, yet she calls Him, "Lord." Yes, even though, on the Cross, she beholds, with tearful eyes, His agony and death--yet even there she salutes Him as Lord! She did so in the dying thief's prayer, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom." And she has done it thousands of times since.

What does Sermon 2912 advise believers who are either overly confident in their standing or constantly terrified of falling?

The sermon teaches that true humility is the safest path, urging believers to acknowledge their limitations: "Your wisest way is to believe yourself neither to be wise nor strong" and to rely on Christ’s strength instead of personal pride. It warns that those who boast of their secure standing are vulnerable to the "fierce wind from the Pit," while those who live in constant fear experience "a strange mingle-mangle of incorrect caution and incorrect doubt." By recalling Paul’s rebuke of the boastful, the sermon offers a "cordial" to revive faint spirits and steadies both the over‑confident and the fearful. [Sermon 2912 — "Comfort for Tried Believers"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2912 — "Comfort for Tried Believers"]
meta.passage:
Your wisest way is to believe yourself neither to be wise nor strong and, therefore, to lie humbly at His feet who can make you both wise and strong--and to look away from yourself up to Him who will keep the feet of His saints. It ought to cool the hot blood of self-conceit in any man to remind him that although he thinks that he stands, it is simply because he has not been tempted as others have been who have fallen! Or if he has been tempted in a way which overthrew them, while he has stood fast, yet, if the temptations were still further increased and he were left to himself, he would find that at the last the fierce wind from the Pit would sweep him off his feet even as it has swept off other men who thought that they could never be moved.

After the Apostle Paul had, by this warning, rebuked the boastings of these who thought they were standing securely, he thought of the far larger number of persons who never think that they can stand, but who are in constant terror lest they should fall. They say they are not the people of God yet, in almost the next breath they say they are afraid that they will lose what they just said they did not have! They sometimes hope that they are saved, yet they quickly doubt if it is so with them--and they are troubled with the fear that even though they are saved, they may yet fall and perish! Their feelings are a strange mingle-mangle of incorrect caution and incorrect doubt! And Paul seems to me in this verse to give them a cordial by which their fainting spirits may be revived.

How does Spurgeon illustrate the superficial understanding of sin through the Pharisee’s example in this sermon?

Spurgeon points out that many people reduce sin to trivial externalities, and he illustrates this by recalling the Pharisee’s definition: "Well," he would say, "it is eating without washing your hands." By highlighting such a shallow view, Spurgeon emphasizes that true sin is far deeper than mere ritual impurity. [Sermon 812 — "The Deep-Seated Character of Sin"]

It is seen, indeed, in us--to deal with ourselves is our main business this morning.

We shall commence by answering the question, WHAT IS SIN? We are always hearing about it. It is constantly dunned into our ears by the preacher. If you ask the Pharisee of old what sin was--"Well," he would say, "it is eating without washing your hands. It is drinking wine without having first of all strained out the gnats, for those insects are unclean, and if you should swallow any of them they will render you defiled."

His repentance dealt with his having touched a Gentile, or having come on the wind side of a Publican. Many in these days have the same notion, but with a variation. We have read of a Spanish bandit, who, when he confessed before his father-confessor, complained that one sin hung with peculiar weight upon his soul that was of peculiar atrocity. He had stabbed a man on a Friday, and a few drops of the blood of the wound had fallen on his lips, by which he had broken the precepts of "Holy Church," in having tasted animal food on a fast day. The murder did not seem to arouse in his conscience any feeling of remorse at all--not one atom--he would have done the same tomorrow.

What mistake does Bolton identify regarding those who think prayer alone is sufficient for Christian duty?

Bolton identifies the error of believing that prayer alone fulfills all Christian obligations. He writes that “Some think they are to doe nothing else but to pray, God hath commanded us to pray, and they thinke they are to doe nothing else, and therefore ever and anon they run to their knees, drop as it were a bead, say over a Pater Noster,” and that this attitude reduces worship to a mere ritual. How does Brooks describe the superiority of Christ's riches over worldly wealth?

Brooks teaches that the riches of Christ far surpass any earthly wealth, noting that "for the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold." He compares a single grain of grace to the gold of Ophir and the silver of the Indies, describing worldly riches as merely "the guts and garbage of the earth." Thus, according to Brooks, even the smallest portion of Christ's riches is superior to all material wealth. [Brooks — Complete Works Vol3]

What distinction does Sermon 2028 make between intellectual belief and the heart’s indwelling regarding spiritual attainments?

The sermon teaches that true spiritual attainments are not merely intellectual assent but the inner work of the heart. It notes that "The attainments which Paul desired for his friends were not beliefs of the head but indwelling of the heart," emphasizing that the divine direction must move the heart before one can navigate the "sweet waters" of higher spiritual wisdom. Thus, the Apostle’s role is to intercede and pray, "The Lord direct your hearts into the love of God," rather than to act as a pilot for the mind alone. [Sermon 2028 — "The Love of God and the Patience of Christ"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2028 — "The Love of God and the Patience of Christ"]
meta.passage:
If so, he would have directed their minds that way at once. But the perception of the heavenlies is only given to heavenly faculties. The attainments which Paul desired for his friends were not beliefs of the head but indwelling of the heart. To return to our figure of sailing up the creeks and rivers into the center of the glorious country--that delicious voyage was only possible to the more refined and spiritual powers of the soul. Those sweet waters could only be navigated by the heart and the heart itself would need Divine direction before it could find the entrance to them.

There is a path which the vulture's eye has not seen and the lion's whelp has not trod--only God sees and knows it. The Beulah country of spiritual wisdom, especially in its higher reaches, is a matter for personal Revelation from God to each one of His own. We are here hopelessly in the dark if we have no light from above. And even with that light we do but see the difficult nature of our way and fail to enter upon it until the light becomes a force and He whom we desire to know directs our hearts into communion with Himself. Yes, yonder are the radiant coasts and the rivers of life up which our boat might sail into the center of "the island of the innocent." Yet our great Apostle does not rush into the office of pilot but humbly acts as intercessor, crying, "The Lord direct your hearts into the love of God."

All this whets our desires! Who would not wish to go where only choice spirits can enter and where these can only come as the Lord directs their hearts?

What does Swinnock say is the only cure for a soul wounded by sin and despair?

Swinnock teaches that no human comforter, physician, or even angel can heal a soul that is wounded by sin; only the divine Word can restore it. He declares, "His word is the onely Balm that can cure the wound ed conscience;" and emphasizes that "it's the same hand that wounded, that alone can cure him; it's the same word that bruised him, that must bind him up." Thus, the only remedy for such a soul is God's spoken Word. [Swinnock — Incomparableness Of God]

What does the Canons of Dort say about the number of decrees of election?

The Canons of Dort affirm that there is a single decree of election for all who will be saved, stating that "There are not various decrees of election, but one and the same decree respecting all those who shall be saved both under the Old and New Testament". This reflects the doctrine that God, from eternity, chose the elect to grace and glory, and that the same decree applies uniformly to believers under both covenants. [Reformed — Canons Of Dort]

What five characteristics of God's grace does Manton enumerate in Works Vol20?

Manton enumerates five distinct characteristics of God's grace. First, he affirms that God "has chosen us in Christ before the foundations of the world," indicating a grace of election. Second, he describes it as "a free grace," emphasizing that it is given without merit. Third, he calls it "a powerful grace to pardon so many sins, and accept us to so great a blessedness: John xii. 32, And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." Fourth, he labels it "a liberal grace," noting that no good thing will be withheld from those who walk uprightly. Finally, he declares it "a glorious grace," so magnificent that "no tongue can express it." [Manton — Works Vol20]

What future scene does the sermon describe in which the Song of Moses will be sung by the believers?

The sermon teaches that "the Song of Moses, the servant of God and of the Lamb, will be sung toward the close of this dispensation" when those who have gained victory over the beast and his image stand on the sea of glass, holding the harps of God, just before the seven last plagues are poured out and God finally overthrows the hosts of Antichrist. [Sermon 1867 — "Untitled Sermon"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1867 — "Untitled Sermon"]
meta.passage:
What an assembly! Millions made up that choir! Though their voices were little tuned to music, yet as they lifted them up, each one throwing his whole strength into the strain, it must have sounded like the noise of many waters, especially when they repeated the refrain, "Sing unto the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider has He thrown into the sea."

We saw just now, in our reading in the 15th Chapter of Revelation, that the Song of Moses, the servant of God and of the Lamb, will be sung toward the close of this dispensation when those who have gotten the victory over the beast and his image shall stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God. Before the seven last plagues shall be poured out upon the earth and God shall overthrow the hosts of Antichrist once and for all, then shall this song be heard, sung, not by the Israelite nation, but by that higher Israel who have escaped by the Grace of God from the power of the spiritual Pharaoh and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb! How sweetly will they together take up the song, "Sing unto the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously! Great and marvelous are Your works, Lord God Almighty."

It is obvious, then, from the plentiful allusions to this song in Holy Scripture, that it is full of deep spiritual significance. It teaches us not only to praise God concerning the literal overthrow of Egypt, but to praise Him concerning the overthrow of all the powers of evil and the final deliverance of all the chosen.

What does Spurgeon say about how God determines the time of a believer's death in his sermon "Crossing the Jordan"?

Spurgeon teaches that the Lord has fixed the hour of a believer’s entrance into rest and that it cannot be altered by human effort or evil intent. He writes that "The Lord often favors His people with notice that the time of their departure is at hand" and emphasizes that "He has fixed the hour of our entrance into rest and it can neither be postponed by skill of physician nor hastened by malice of foe." Thus, whether death comes suddenly or after a long season, the timing is divinely appointed and the believer need not fear being unprepared. [Sermon 2039 — "Crossing the Jordan"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2039 — "Crossing the Jordan"]
meta.passage:
For within three days you shall pass over this Jordan." The Lord often favors His people with notice that the time of their departure is at hand. He has fixed the hour of our entrance into rest and it can neither be postponed by skill of physician nor hastened by malice of foe. No Satanic force can hurl us to the grave before our time--

"Plagues and death around us fly, Till He bids we cannot die."

In due time there comes a whisper in the ear of the Believer, "Rise up and come away." Mr. Bunyan describes the pilgrims as tarrying on the shore of that river which parted them from the celestial country until a post came to one and another, announcing that the silver cord must be loosed and the golden bowl be broken. Father Honest and Mr. Ready-to-Halt and Christiana and the rest of them received each one a call from the hill country and passed over the black water to the golden strand--where the shining ones stood to meet them.

Perhaps some of us may get no such summons. For we may be taken away on a sudden. Many good people daily pray against sudden death and there are legitimate reasons for so doing. But to a child of God it is of small consequence, for death will never find him unprepared if he is living in communion with God. If we walk in the light, as He is in the light,

an abundant entrance will be ministered to us into eternal glory even if we should fall dead in a moment. The change would simply mean going from the lower room of our Father's house into an upper chamber more bright and beauti-ful--but still a part of the same house.

A Christian's heart is to be the presence chamber of the
 blessed Trinity; and shall not holiness to the Lord be written upon it?
 Believers are children of God the Father, members of God the Son, and
 temples of God the Holy Ghost; and shall they not be holy? Holiness is
 the badge and livery of God's people. "The people of thy holiness"
 (Isaiah lxiii. 18). As chastity distinguishes a virtuous woman from a
 harlot, so holiness distinguishes the godly from the wicked. It is a
 holy calling; "For God hath nor called us unto uncleanness, but unto
 holiness" (1 Thess. iv. 7). Let not any man say he is called of God,
 that lives in sin. Has God called you to be a swearer, to be a
 drunkard? Nay, let not the merely moral person say he is effectually
 called. What is civility without sanctity? It is but a dead carcass
 strewed with flowers. The king's picture stamped upon brass will not go
 current for gold. The merely moral man looks as if he had the King of
 heaven's image stamped upon him, but he is no better than counterfeit
 metal, which will not pass for current with God.

 (iii.) It is an irresistible call. When God calls a man by His grace,
 he cannot but come. You may resist the minister's call, but you cannot
 the Spirit's call. The finger of the blessed Spirit can write upon a
 heart of stone, as once He wrote His laws upon tables of stone. God's
 words are creating words; when He said "Let there be light, there was
 light"; and when He says, "Let there be faith", it shall be so. When
 God called Paul, he answered to the call.

Why does Spurgeon say God created creatures, according to Sermon 115?

Spurgeon teaches that the ultimate reason God created creatures is for his own pleasure and glory, stating that "He made them for his own pleasure and for his own glory." He also affirms that "He made all things for himself and by himself," and he applies the same principle to the work of salvation. [Sermon 115 — "Why Are Men Saved?"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 115 — "Why Are Men Saved?"]
meta.passage:
Whatever other replies men may propound, no other can be really sound. If they will for one moment consider that there was a time when God had no creatures—when he dwelt alone, the mighty maker of ages, glorious in an uncreated solitude, divine in his eternal loneliness—"I am and there is none beside me"—can any one answer this question—Why did God make creatures to exist?—in any other way than by answering it thus: "He made them for his own pleasure and for his own glory." You may say he made them for his creatures; but we answer, there were then no creatures to make them for. We admit that the answer may be a sound one now. God makes the harvest for his creatures; he hangs the sun in the firmament to bless his creatures with light and sunshine; he bids the moon walk I her course by night, to cheer the darkness of his creatures upon earth. But the first answer, going back to the origin of all things, can be nothing else than this: "For his pleasure they are and were created." "He made all things for himself and by himself."

Now, this which holds good in the works of creation, holds equally good in the works of salvation.

According to Byfield’s Marrow Of The Oracles, what is the proper way for believers to show love toward the godly?

Byfield teaches that believers must serve the godly wholeheartedly, as if they were serving themselves or their own kin, and must employ their spiritual gifts for the good of others. He writes that “we should doe all things we vn dertake for them, with all side lity and care”, urging care for the godly’s profit as members of the mystical body of Christ. The passage further advises using gifts such as knowledge, prayer, and exhortation to benefit the community and to help one another by prayer, whether absent or present. Byfield thus outlines the rules that concern the manifestation of love to the godly. [Byfield — Marrow Of The Oracles]

What does the Boston passage “Crook In The Lot” advise believers to do when their burdens are uneven and cannot be evened out?

Boston teaches that believers should seek the grace that matches their difficulty, trusting that “Grace proportioned to the trial is what we should aim at; getting that, though the crook be not evened, we are even hands with it.” By keeping their eyes on the eternal rest and weight of glory, they are to “bear it, Patiently, without firing and fretting, or murmuring,” and avoid resisting God, “not fight against God, and so kick against the pricks.” This posture allows the crook in their lot to be balanced by divine grace. [Boston — Crook In The Lot]

According to the sermon, who is the Hosea 11:9 text primarily addressed to?

The sermon explains that the passage is directed specifically to "sinners of the deepest dye," emphasizing that God’s mercy reaches even those most entrenched in sin. It notes that the text, which declares "I will not execute the fierceness of My anger; I will not return to destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not man," is meant to comfort and invite the most wayward sinners to receive divine pardon. [Sermon 366 — "The Silver Trumpet"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 366 — "The Silver Trumpet"]
meta.passage:
Oh that we knew the meaning of that text, where God says, "I will not execute the fierceness of My anger; I will not return to destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not man" (Hosea 11:9.) He acts in everything, not as a king gives to a king, or as some right royal heart acts towards the needy, but as a God! There is none who can come near to Him; as He is surpassing in His Glory so that mortal eyes cannot behold it, so He is excelling in His love and Grace, so that mortal comprehension can never grasp, comprehend, or fathom the infinity of His mercy! Keeping mercy with thousands, showing pity to multitudes--who is a God like He, passing by transgression, iniquity and sin?

My text shall at once introduce itself. It is a great text, indeed--specially meant for sinners of the deepest dye. I pray that the energy and power of the Spirit may now open the door of all our hearts, that God's mercy may enter in. Four things we will attempt to do this morning. First, we will remark that the text is addressed to sinners of the deepest dye. Secondly, it contains in it an invitation to reason of the most prevailing power. Thirdly, it promises pardons of the fullest force. And, fourthly, it presents to us a time of the most solemn significance.

First, then, our text is addressed to SINNERS OF THE DEEPEST DYE. Some of my Brothers are greatly scandalized by the general invitations which I am in the habit of giving to sinners, as sinners. Some of them go the length of asserting that there are no universal invitations in the Word of God.

How does Beveridge argue that the biblical promises concerning the blessing and the everlasting throne demonstrate Christ’s true human nature against the claims of the Marcionites and Manichees?

Beveridge teaches that the scriptural promises are anchored in earthly lineage rather than a heavenly or aerial existence, thereby confirming that Christ assumed genuine human flesh. He writes, "The blessing is not promised in a heavenly seed, or the mask of a man, but the seed of Abra.hajn and .Tnf.nb ; nor is the everlasting throne promised to an aerial man, but to the Son of David, and the fruit of his loins." This contrast shows that the blessings and throne are tied to the seed of Abraham and the Son of David, refuting the notion of a phantom or purely celestial Christ. [Institutes — Institutes Beveridge Vol2]

Why does Henry say that even those who have ample reason to rejoice can still be cast down in sorrow?

Henry teaches that believers who have much cause for joy are often "cast down and in sorrow, and not altogether without cause" because they are living in "This state of probation and preparation is a mixed state," which serves as a trial and exercise of various graces, allowing God's power to be praised in keeping the balance. [Henry — Communicants Companion]

What distinction did Placaeus draw about the imputation of Adam’s guilt, and how did the National Synod of Charenton respond to his view?

Dabney teaches that Placaeus tried to evade the Synod’s censure by inventing a two‑fold distinction: he denied an " antecedent and immediate imputation " of Adam’s guilt while affirming a " mediate and subsequent imputation" that he claimed to hold. In reality, the Synod condemned his denial of any imputation, noting that “The charge made in the National Synod of Charenton, was, that Placaeus had denied all imputation of Adam's guilt, and had made original sin consist exclusively in subjective depravity.” Thus, Dabney concludes that Placaeus’s distinction was a strategic move to avoid condemnation rather than a legitimate theological solution. [Systematic — Dabney Systematic Theology]

What was Calvin’s first action regarding church governance after returning to the city, as described in Tracts Vol1?

In Tracts Vol1, Calvin records that his initial step was to secure civil approval for a biblically based church structure, noting that “the first thing he did was to obtain the consent of the Senate to a form of ecclesiastical polity, which was agreeable to the Word of God.” This demonstrates his priority of establishing a polity aligned with Scripture before addressing other challenges. [Calvin — Tracts Vol1]

What specific possessions and relationships does Spurgeon say Abraham had to abandon when he obeyed God's call in Sermon 261?

Spurgeon explains that Abraham was required to abandon a great many personal ties and material blessings. He notes that Abraham "left behind him all the associationof his youth, the house in which he had been trained, the family with which he had been nursed, all those whom he had known and with whom he had taken sweet counsel" and that he also relinquished "his native country" along with "a considerable property in flocks and herds," the ancestral dwelling house, the pastures that fed his and his father's flocks, and even his "vine and his fig tree." All of these were forsaken as he journeyed into an unknown wilderness. [Sermon 261 — "The Call of Abraham"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 261 — "The Call of Abraham"]
meta.passage: We shall notice first what Abraham left, and then where Abraham went; the trial is made up of these two things. What had he to leave? He had to leave behind him those who were exceeding dear to him. It is true that just after his first call, his own father, Terah, died, having gone a part of the way with Abraham and detained Abraham a little while by sickness. Abraham then went on his way obedient to the Lord's command. Nevertheless, he left behind him all the associationof his youth, the house in which he had been trained, the family with which he had been nursed, all those whom he had known and with whom he had taken sweet counsel; and he must go forth into exile from the family of his love. He left behind him his native country, and to a patriot that is no small struggle—to leave all the associations of one's country, and bear with us one's native songs to be sung in distant valleys. Many a man has felt keenly enough the separation from home and kindred, and next to that, the sad banishment from his native land. Besides, we all know with what inconvenience Abraham must have removed. He had a considerable property in flocks and herds, and probably had the ancestral dwelling house in which to reside. He must leave all these, and he must also leave the fair pastures wherein his flocks and his father's flocks had been fed, and he must wend his way into the wilderness. He must give up all agricultural pursuits, renounce his vine and his fig tree, and go his way, he knew not whither, to a land which to him was as unknown as the valley of the shadow of death.

What does Brooks say the 'sea of glass mingled with fire' represents in his vision of the final overthrow of Antichrist?

Brooks explains that the phrase "sea of glass mingled with fire" is a symbolic picture of the fiery trials and dreadful persecutions that Antichrist will bring upon sincere and faithful Christians. What distinction does the sermon make between merely receiving Christ’s teachings and truly receiving Christ Himself?

The sermon teaches that believers may accept Christ’s precepts and ordinances, but true reception involves the inward acceptance of His Person, Godhead, and humanity. It emphasizes that "There is a vast difference between the outward reception of the Doctrine, or the ordinance, and the inward reception of Christ," and that only those who have received Christ can comprehend this mystery. [Sermon 3030 — "A Consistent Walk for Time to Come"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3030 — "A Consistent Walk for Time to Come"]
meta.passage:
The first point to which I would particularly direct your attention is the personality of this reception. Believers have, it is true, received Christ's words. They prize every precept, they value every Doctrine, but this is not all. They have received Christ Himself. While they have received Christ's ordinances and are not slow to walk in obedience to the things which He has commanded, they do not stay here. They have received Christ Himself--His Person, His Godhead and His Humanity. They have "received Christ Jesus the Lord." And, mark you, there is a very great distinction here--and also a great mystery. A great distinction, I say, for there are some who do, I think, wholly believe the doctrines which Christ has taught, and are profoundly orthodox, full of an earnest controversial spirit for the faith once delivered to the saints and yet, for all that, they do not seem to have received Him, the very Christ of God! And, truly, there are many who have received both Baptism and the Lord's Supper, yet, despite what any may say, we believe that they have not received Christ, but are still as great strangers to Him as though they had only passed through the rites common to mankind, or the rites in which heathens indulge! There is a vast difference between the outward reception of the Doctrine, or the ordinance, and the inward reception of Christ.

We also said that herein is a mystery--such a mystery that only he who has received Christ can understand. The preacher cannot tell you what it is to receive Christ.

According to Sermon 3447, what three ways does the promise “I am with you” describe Christ’s relationship with believers?

Spurgeon teaches that the promise “I am with you” is to be understood in three complementary ways. First, it denotes Christ’s presence with the Church, not merely as a distant observer but as the very One who dwells among His people. Second, it conveys His sympathy, because “I am with you" expresses His feeling for us and His compassion toward our suffering. Third, it signifies succor and co‑operation, meaning that Jesus works alongside believers, exerting His power in connection with theirs. By combining presence, sympathy, and co‑operation, the sermon shows the full comfort of Christ’s abiding help. [Sermon 3447 — "A Present Helper"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3447 — "A Present Helper"]
meta.passage:
Why, one of His farewell words was this, "Lo, I am with you always"--a dear and blessed legacy to His children who are still in banishment below! And when John, in Patmos, had a vision of Jesus in His Glory, where, do you think, did he see Him? Did he see Him as standing before the Throne of God, or in any position of Glory? Yes, he did, but first of all he said, "I saw Him walking among the golden candlesticks." Now, he tells us, these golden candelabra represented the Churches--and Jesus Christ was pictured even as a glorified Savior, holding the seven stars in His right hand and walking among the seven golden candlesticks! Hence I gather that the truest comfort of the Church is for Christ to be with us--and that one of the highest joys of Jesus is to be with His people!

I shall ask you, now, to consider the grateful fact that Jesus is with Believers. The words, "I am with you," may be taken in three ways--and the three must be combined to get the whole of their sense.

"I am with you." This implies His Presence. That would not be enough--a person is not with us if he is merely in the same place as a spectator. "I am with you" expresses His sympathy. He is not here as a stranger, but He is here feeling for us, compassionating with us. "I am with you" has a yet deeper significance. It involves succor. He is working with you-- on the same side--exerting His power in connection with yours. Put the three together, and you get presence, sympathy, co-operation, to interpret the meaning.

How does the sermon define the spiritual category called “young men” in the church?

The sermon explains that “young men” are those believers who have outgrown the stage of being "babes in Grace" but have not yet reached the maturity of "fathers" in the church. It emphasizes that the term is metaphorical, referring to spiritual growth rather than chronological age, noting that "young men" can include both youthful individuals who are spiritually mature and older persons who remain spiritually infantile. Thus, the classification is based on the work of the Spirit in a believer’s eternal life, not on the fleeting, dying life. [Sermon 1715 — "A Description of Young Men in Christ"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1715 — "A Description of Young Men in Christ"]
meta.passage:
Lifting his head from that dear bosom which gave him unexampled rest, he whispers, "I write unto you young men." Looking down from that favored place which he now occupies so near to the Throne of the Lamb, he looks over the battlements of Heaven upon us and cries, "I have written unto you, young men." In the Christian Church there is an order of Christians who have grown so much that they can no longer be called, "babes in Grace," but yet they are not so far matured that they can exactly be called, "fathers." These, who form the middle class of the spiritual-minded, are styled "young men."

Understand that the Apostle is not writing, here, to any according to their bodily age--he is using human age as a metaphor and figure for representing growth in the spiritual life. Age, according to the flesh, often differs much from the condition of the spirit--many old men are still no more than "babes." Some children in years are, even now, "young men" in Grace, while not a few young men are "fathers " in the Church while young in years. God has endowed certain of His servants with great Grace and made them mature in their youth--such were Joseph, Samuel, David, Josiah and Timothy. It is not age according to the family register that we are now to speak about, but age according to the Lamb's Book of Life.

Grace is a matter of growth and, therefore, we have among us babes, young men and fathers, whose position is not reckoned according to this fleeting, dying life, but according to that eternal life which has been worked in them by the Spirit of God.

What does Sibbes say about the effect of God’s all‑seeing eye on a person’s inner thoughts and actions?

Sibbes teaches that the very thought of God’s constant observation should keep a believer from entertaining sinful ideas. He writes, "If we had knowledge that such an eye of God is fixed upon us in all places, in all our affections and actions", and adds, "Men are not afraid of their thoughts, affections, desires, and inward delights of their soul, because there is no eye of justice upon them." Because the divine eye watches every affection and intention, a person would be as afraid to think evil as to do evil, leading to greater holiness. [Sibbes — Works Vol02]

What does Sermon 1268 say about Paul’s own handwriting in his letter to Philemon?

The sermon observes that although Paul normally dictated his letters, the Epistle to Philemon contains a passage written by his own hand, noting that "I, Paul, have written it with my own hand. I will repay it." It points out that even when inspiration guides the message, the apostle exercised careful thought and chose each word purposefully, urging believers to adopt a compassionate spirit toward those who have erred. [Sermon 1268 — "The Story of a Runaway Slave"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1268 — "The Story of a Runaway Slave"]
meta.passage:
And when Paul thought it right that he should return to his master, Philemon, he took a deal of trouble to compose a letter of apology for him, a letter which shows long thinking, since every word is well selected. Although the Holy Spirit dictated it, Inspiration does not prevent a man's exercising thought and care on what he writes. Every word is chosen for a purpose. If he had been pleading for himself, he could not have pleaded more earnestly or wisely. Paul, as you know, was not accustomed to write letters with his own hand, but dictated to a secretary.

It is supposed that he had an affection of the eyes and, therefore, when he did write, he used large capital letters, as he says in one of the Epistles, "You see how large a letter I have written unto you with my own hand." The Epistle was not a large one, but he probably alluded to the largeness of the characters which he was obliged to use whenever he, himself, wrote. This letter to Philemon, at least part of it, was not dictated, but was written by his own hand. See the 19th verse. "I, Paul, have written it with my own hand. I will repay it." It is the only note of hand which I recall in Scripture, but there it is--an I O U for whatever amount Onesimus may have stolen!

Let us cultivate a large-hearted spirit and sympathize with the people of God, especially with new converts, if we find them in trouble through past wrongdoing. If anything needs setting right, do not let us condemn them off-hand and say, "You have been stealing from your master, have you?

Why does Beveridge consider the view that faith is merely an assent a despiser of God can receive from Scripture to be absurd?

Beveridge teaches that the claim that faith is simply an intellectual agreement is absurd because true faith is a gift of the Holy Spirit and a matter of the heart, not something a person can generate by his own strength. He points out that critics "faith is an assent with which any despiser of God may receive what is delivered by Scripture," yet he argues that one must first determine whether any one can by his own strength acquire faith, or whether the Spirit makes it the witness of adoption. For this reason he emphasizes that "assent itself ... is more a matter of the heart than the head, of the affection than the intellect," and therefore true faith is the "obedience of faith" that the Lord prefers above all other service. [Institutes — Institutes Beveridge Vol2]

What does Sermon 2446 say about the ingenuity of great faith versus little faith?

The sermon teaches that true, great faith displays a creative ingenuity that distinguishes it from superficial belief. It points to the Canaanite woman's response to Christ as evidence, noting that she bore severe trials yet persisted, and the Lord affirmed her by saying, "O woman, great is your faith,". By contrast, the sermon warns that "Little faith always lacks ingenuity-- it must have everything very plain or else it cannot move at all." Thus, according to the sermon, genuine faith is marked by resourceful confidence, while shallow faith remains plain and ineffective. [Sermon 2446 — "Carte Blanche"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2446 — "Carte Blanche"]
meta.passage:
We are glad when those who have been brought up religiously and morally are led to believe in Christ, but we are often more astonished when the immoral-- those who have previously known nothing of true godliness--are enabled by Divine Grace to exercise great faith in Christ. "O woman, great is your faith," said our Lord, for it was great even apart from her being a Gentile, for it had been sorely tried. Trials of faith from disciples are often very severe, but the disciples had put her aside and even besought their Lord to, "Send her away."

But trials of faith from the Master, Himself, are still more severe. To have Christ's deaf ear and dumb lips--this was a trial, indeed, and worse than that, to have rough words from such a loving and tender Teacher as He was, and even to be called a dog by the great Shepherd of Israel and to be told that it was not right to give her the children's bread--these were heavy tests of her confidence! But she had such faith that she bore up under all and still pressed her suit with the Son of David, the Lord of Mercy! We cannot but feel that Christ did her justice when He said, "O woman, great is your faith."

Our Savior seems to have been especially struck with the ingenuity of her faith. Little faith always lacks ingenuity-- it must have everything very plain or else it cannot move at all.
