What does the sermon say John the Baptist declares about Jesus?

The sermon records that John the Baptist declares Jesus to be the sacrificial Lamb, proclaiming “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” It emphasizes that this declaration is a practical truth meant to prompt repentance, fruit‑bearing works, and a life aligned with God's redemptive purpose. [Sermon 1987 — "Behold the Lamb of God"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1987 — "Behold the Lamb of God"]
meta.passage:
Lifting up his hand and pointing to Jesus, he cried, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." He did not say, "Behold the great Exemplar"--no doubt he would have said that in due season. He did not even say, "Behold the King and Leader of a new dispensation"--that fact he, by no means, would have denied, but would have gloried in it. Still, the first point that he dwells upon, and that which wins his enthusiasm is, "Behold the Lamb of God." John the Baptist views Him as the Propitiation for sin and so he cries, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world."

My Brothers and Sisters, we may depend upon it that this must be a very practical Truth of God, for John was preeminently practical. What is the sum and substance of his teaching but, "Repent. Bring forth fruits meet for repentance. The axe is laid unto the root of the trees"? He has a word for everybody that comes--even the Roman soldiers are told to be content with their rations. John is no theorist or quibbler about dogma. He deals with life and character and demands works meet for repentance. Yet he makes a great point of our Lord's being the Sacrifice for sin. This, indeed, is the text of his life-sermon! Rest assured that there is something wonderfully practical about that Truth of God! And those who becloud it under the notion of being practical are laying aside the best instrument of doing good to men.

How does Spurgeon describe Jesus’ continued empathy for believers after He has "is passed into the heavens"?

Spurgeon teaches that believers may approach God’s throne with boldness because they "We have a High Priest." He stresses that even after Christ has ascended, He has not abandoned the feelings of human weakness: He “retains to the fullest the fellow feelings which His life of humiliation has developed in Him.” Thus, although Jesus is “is passed into the heavens,” He still experiences the infirmities of His people, remaining near‑kin and full of boundless love toward them. [Sermon 2148 — "The Tenderness of Jesus"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2148 — "The Tenderness of Jesus"]
meta.passage:
Every blessing of the Covenant is prized in proportion as it is had-- "We have a High Priest." I pray you, never talk of the blessings and Doctrines of Grace as matters apart from personal possession, but seek habitually to enjoy and experience them! That was a grand exclamation of Thomas, "My Lord, and my God," and this is a sweet word for the saints--"We have a High Priest."

Beloved, come boldly to the Throne of God for you have a High Priest. Grasp firmly by faith the choice favors which your interest in the Lord Jesus secures to you. It is precious to reflect that Jesus, as High Priest, is still ours, though, according to the text, He "is passed into the heavens." He does not forget us now that He has passed through the lower heavens into the Heaven of heavens where He reigns supreme in His Father's Glory. He is still touched with a feeling of our infirmities. Though He has left behind Him all pain, suffering and infirmity, He retains to the fullest the fellow feelings which His life of humiliation has developed in Him.

"The Man is near of kin unto us" and no difference of situation or condition has changed His kinship or the boundless love which goes with it. Our Joseph, though Lord of all Egypt, is our Brother, still, and beneath the vestments of a king there beats the heart of love. Think of our High Priest as not having laid aside that breastplate of His on which our names are engraved, nor the "two onyx stones, set in pouches of gold," which He wore upon His shoulders, inscribed in the same manner.

What are the four ways Augustine says God is for us as presented in Spurgeon’s Sermon 580?

Spurgeon teaches that Augustine outlines four senses in which God is for us: He is for us because He has predestinated us, He is for us because He has called us, He is for us because He has justified us, and He is for us because He has virtually glorified us and will actually do so. As the sermon affirms, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” [Sermon 580 — "God Is With Us"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 580 — "God Is With Us"]
meta.passage:
But if through the sprinkled blood you can say that you are reconciled unto God, then take the full meaning of this text and feast upon it and be blessed, for "If God is for us, who can be against us?" We shall handle the text thus and may the Holy Spirit make it profitable--how is God for us? Secondly, who are against us? And thirdly, who are not against us?

First, HOW IS GOD FOR US? Augustine, in his notes upon the verses preceding our text has very beautifully said that God is for us according to the preceding words of the chapter in four senses. Look back a verse or two and you will find it. He is for us, for He has predestinated us. He is for us for He has called us. He is for us for He has justified us. He is for us because He has virtually glorified us and will actually do so. To the people of God here are four very prolific subjects of thought.

God is for us, because, according to the words of the Apostle He has predestinated His people to be conformed to the image of His own dear Son. Now, if God has predestinated us to eternal life, who can be against us? Must not the predestinating decree of God take effect? If God has determined it, who shall disannul it? If God has said it shall be, who is he that shall stay His hand, or resist the Omnipotent fiat of the Most High? He said, "Let there be light: and there was light." He bade the world spring out of nothing and forth it came. All things obey Him. Heaven adores Him. Hell trembles at Him. No creature can resist Him.

What description does Spurgeon give of the feast in his sermon "Good Cheer for Christians"?

Spurgeon teaches that the feast described in the sermon is composed of the finest provisions, describing them as "They are fat things, but they are also fat things full of marrow." He explains that this abundance represents the Gospel’s blessings, the "best of the best" that God provides for humanity, and that the Lord will make a feast for all people. [Sermon 846 — "Good Cheer for Christians"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 846 — "Good Cheer for Christians"]
meta.passage:
He spoke of the marriage supper of the king, who said, "My oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready." And it did not seem as if He could even complete the beauty of the parable of the prodigal son without the killing of the fat calf and feasting and music and dancing! As a festival on earth is looked forward to and looked back upon as an oasis and a desert of time, so the Gospel of Jesus Christ is to the soul its sweet release from bondage and distress--its mirth and joy!

Upon this subject we intend to speak this morning, hoping to be helped by the great Master of the feast. Our first head will be the feast. The second will be the banqueting hall in this mountain. The third will be the Host--"The Lord shall make a feast." And the fourth head shall be the guests--He shall make it "unto all people."

First, then, we have to consider THE FEAST. It is described as consisting of viands of the best, no, of the best of the best! They are fat things, but they are also fat things full of marrow. Wines are provided of the most delicious and invigorating kind--wines on the lees, which retain their aroma, their strength, and their flavor--but these are most ancient and rare, having been so long kept that they have become well-refined. By long standing they have purified and clarified themselves--and brought themselves to the highest degree of brightness and excellence. The best of the best God has provided in the Gospel for the sons of men!

Let us attentively survey the blessings of the Gospel and observe that they are fat things, and fat things full of marrow.

According to Spurgeon in “The Main Matter,” what does he say about the purpose and meaning of each individual act of Christ?

Spurgeon teaches that every single act of Jesus is not a trivial occurrence but a divine sign that conveys a wealth of instruction. He emphasizes that Christ’s life was “full of Grace and the Truths of God,” and that each deed was a manifestation of “the fullness of the Godhead bodily.” As he notes, the Apostle recorded that there were “many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of His disciples,” indicating that every movement of the Lord served as a sign pointing beyond itself to an “ocean of doctrine without bottom or shore.” Thus, Spurgeon holds that the whole of Christ’s recorded life is deliberately preserved so believers may be enriched and become “rich to the Glory of God, and full to the blessing of our fellow men.” [Sermon 1631 — "The Main Matter"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1631 — "The Main Matter"]
meta.passage:
He did not display a multitude of feeblenesses, but each individual outcome of His life was grand enough to have been a marvel if considered by itself! As was the Doer, in whom "dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily," such were the deeds--they, also, were full of Grace and the Truths of

God!

There was a fullness of Divine wisdom, Grace and power about each act of Jesus. Hence the Apostle, here, speaks of the Lord's acts as signs--"many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of His disciples." There was a mass of instruction in all our Lord's movements. Nothing about Him was trivial. He preached by His entire life, preached a marvelous array of Truths and preached them with living freshness! Never is He twice the same, though always the same. When we find Him repeating His discourses, as we sometimes do, if the Sermon on the Mount sounds like the Sermon on the Plain, yet a different drift, aim and tone create a singular variety. Each separate act of the Lord is a sign of something beyond itself and the whole of the acts put together display an ocean of doctrine without bottom or shore.

What a Christ was this! Oh that His Spirit may dwell in us, that our lives, also, may be rich and full! Rich to the Glory of God, and full to the blessing of our fellow men. Yet, dear Friends, though the whole of Christ's life has not been written, we perceive in our text that what has been recorded is the most useful part of it and that it was preserved for our benefit.

What lamentation of love and expression of ingratitude does Spurgeon point out in Sermon 2782?

Spurgeon teaches that the people’s response to divine chastisement is one of complaint rather than confession, and he underscores the prophetic lamentation of love by quoting, "I have loved you, says the Lord." He then records their insensibility with the rebuke, "Yet you say, In what way have You loved us?" From this, Spurgeon exhorts his listeners to awaken their consciences, repent, and offer genuine confession before God. [Sermon 2782 — "Love's Lamentation"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2782 — "Love's Lamentation"]
meta.passage:
They were fretting and fuming against God instead of striking out boldly at their sins--complaining of the severity of the Divine chastisement rather than confessing the iniquity by which they had brought the rod upon themselves!

So God sent His servant Malachi, the last of a long train of Prophets, to seek to bring them to repentance--to try to touch their hearts and consciences by reminding them of His manifold favor and of their base ingratitude towards Him who had treated them so graciously and with such undeserved mercy. This is to be the subject of my discourse. I want, if I can, to get at men's hearts. I shall not have much to say by way of instruction--I want, rather, to speak so as to impress and awaken my hearers, seeking to set your consciences at work so that all of us--for I hope there will be something to touch us all--may be compelled to bow before God in true repentance and with genuine confession of sin.

The text seems to me to contain two things and to suggest a third. First, here is the lamentation of love--"I have loved you, says the Lord." Secondly, here is the insensibility of ingratitude--"Yet you say, In what way have You loved us?" They would not see any signs and tokens of God's love, for they did not believe in it.

How does Boyce describe the role of good works in the believer’s sanctification?

Boyce teaches that good works are a secondary means of sanctification, stating that "the good works of the Christian, furnish another secondary means for his sanctification." He clarifies that these works are not perfect in a legal sense, but are the outward actions that result from a life lived through the Spirit. Moreover, Boyce notes that "These good works are the result of sanctification ; but, in their performance, they naturally become the means of further sanctification," indicating that while they flow from prior sanctification, they also serve to deepen it when performed in connection with the truth of God. [Systematic — Boyce Abstract Of Systematic Theology]

What does Rutherford say about the importance of liberal education for the moral development of kings?

Rutherford argues that liberal education is crucial for shaping the character of monarchs, observing that "the tender minds of kings may be properly seasoned from theirjvery cradle !" He further notes that the impact of a ruler is profound, because "the blessings conferred by good kings on their subjects are so numerous, and the calamities originating with bad princes are, on the other hand, equally numerous." Accordingly, he stresses the need for careful instruction of princes to safeguard the realm. [Rutherford — Lex Rex]

What conditions does the passage say allow a believer who falls into sin to remain within God's mercy and election?

The author teaches that a fall into sin does not jeopardize election when the sin is not voluntary, is not taken with complacency, and the sinner promptly repents. Moreover, the sin must be "clearly discerned," "sensibly bewailed," "strongly resisted," and "dayly laboured, and prayed against." In his own words, "if you fall into sin with these ingredients, you are not with in the compasse of Gods mercy to save." Under these circumstances, the sin is not damning nor an impediment to election. [Love — Effectual Calling]

What contrasting visual descriptions of Christ does the sermon use to illustrate both His antiquity and His perpetual youth?

The sermon points out that John observed Christ with "His head and His hairs were white like wool, as white as snow," to signify His antiquity, while the spouse described Him as having "His locks are bushy and black as a raven," to indicate His perpetual youth and unfading beauty. These opposing images are presented as evidence of the strange and wondrous nature of Christ’s person. [Sermon 2614 — "Strange Things"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2614 — "Strange Things"]
meta.passage:
No man ever spent a day with Jesus Christ without being filled with the sight of strange things! No man ever entered into communion with the Lord Jesus without being delighted with wonders of love, of mercy, of Divine Grace, of the Truths of God, of goodness for, while His Gospel is the old, old Gospel, yet it always has a new face upon it and is continually fresh and new--it never gets stale! We read of our Lord that when John saw Him, "His head and His hairs were white like wool, as white as snow," to denote His antiquity. And yet the spouse said of Him, "His locks are bushy and black as a raven," as if to indicate His perpetual youth, His unfailing strength and His unfading beauty. Believe me, dear Friends, if you want to see that which is truly strange, you must get into that spiritual realm where Christ is acknowledged as King, the new Heaven and new earth wherein dwell righteousness.

If you want to continue to be astounded, amazed, astonished, filled with holy awe, you must come and be familiar with the Savior, His person, His work, His offices and everything that has to do with Him and, when you have become familiar with all these things, then you will have to say constantly, "We have seen strange things today. Something has occurred that has surprised even us who have grown used to surprises.

What does Shepard explain as the ultimate purpose of the Law and its relation to love?

Shepard explains that the Law is intended not as a burdensome rule for the righteous but as a means to foster charity and love toward God and neighbor. He states that "The Law is very good, when used lawfully, that is, for this End, and out of these Principles, ver. 8." and further emphasizes that "Love being the End and Scope of the Law." Thus, obedience to the Law should flow from a heart filled with love, rather than from mere external compulsion. [Shepard — Sound Believer]

What justification does Calvin give for infant baptism in his Tracts Vol3?

Calvin argues that infant baptism is justified because infants belong to the covenant community of the Church, and God acknowledges those presented by the ministry as already his own. He writes, "Infants are baptized because they are of the household of the Church." He adds, "Paedo- baptism rests on this ground, that God recognises those who are presented to him by our ministry as already his own." Thus, baptism is not dependent on external signs but on the child's inclusion in God's household. [Calvin — Tracts Vol3]

What does Sibbes say about the danger of trusting in good works?

Sibbes teaches that confidence in good works is detrimental because it shifts trust from God to human effort, leading to self‑reliance and spiritual weakness. He writes, "good works are good, but confidence in them is hurtful", and explains that such confidence "deceives us, but hurts us with the splinters" and ultimately leaves the soul dependent on its own frailty rather than on Christ’s sustaining power. Therefore, true trust must be placed in God alone, who alone makes any good work effective. [Sibbes — Souls Conflict]

According to Sermon 3415, how does the love of God affect a believer’s attitude toward things that offend God?

The sermon teaches that a true love for God makes a believer regard anything that offends God as an offense to himself. It states that “EVERYTHING WHICH OFFENDS GOD OUGHT TO OFFEND US.” Therefore, if a heart is reconciled to God, it will naturally reject what God hates, using that rejection as a sign of genuine faith. [Sermon 3415 — "Right-hand Sins"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 3415 — "Right-hand Sins"]
meta.passage:
We shall have to urge upon you the most strenuous giving up of sin and that which leads to sin--but this, not as a means of salvation--but as a result of faith and as an evidence that salvation is truly possessed--as the sign and token, the proof and the earnest of the good work of the Holy Spirit within the soul. We shall begin, therefore, with this short assertion which will serve as our first point of thought--

EVERYTHING WHICH OFFENDS GOD OUGHT TO OFFEND US.

You notice the text says, "If your hand offends you." We might read it, "Makes you to offend God." The two expressions ought, in our experience, mean the same thing, for everything which offends God does offend every truly gracious heart. That short statement will serve as a touchstone for us all to know whether we are reconciled to God or not. Remember, if you truly love God, it must be so--that that which is hateful to Him will be hateful to you. Where two hearts are bound together in the bonds of love, they are quite sure to endeavor to remove everything out of the way that would cause pain to either. You cannot love me if you favor my enemies. You can have no affection for me if you delight to thrust before me that which vexes my spirit and grieves my heart. True love feels a sympathy with the person loved and learns to put away that which is obnoxious. Now say, Heart, do you put away from yourself that which God hates?

What reason does Witsius give for Christ’s intense suffering and terror before God’s tribunal?

Witsius explains that Christ’s suffering was not merely due to sympathy with humanity’s frailty or the horror of death, but because he bore the sins of the whole world and stood before an inexorable divine justice. He writes that “This great trouble and agony did not ai:;^ife only from” the sympathy of the flesh, but from his bearing the sins of all humanity before the “awful tribunal of God” where “the Judge himself armed with his incomprehenfible vengeance” was ready to exact full satisfaction. Thus, Christ endured the full weight of divine wrath to atone for mankind. [Systematic — Witsius Economy Of The Covenants Vol1]

What does the author of the Greenham Works say believers should do when they notice the first motion of sin?

The author teaches that believers must strike at the first motion of sin and eliminate it before it becomes fully formed. He writes, "We must destroy the broode, whilest it is in hatching, and wound sinne before it haue receiued a perfect shape." By destroying the brood while it is still hatching, they prevent sin from taking a perfect shape and keep reason on their side. [Greenham — Works]

How does Sibbes characterize the dominant preaching style of his era in Works Vol01?

Sibbes observes that the dominant preaching of his era had become a "frivolous, florid eloquence, that boasted itself on its deftly-turned tropes, its high-flown paraphrases of the classics, especially Seneca and Cicero, and the Fathers," likening the multiplied quotations to "purple patches on a thread-bare robe" and suggesting that such mannered discourse was merely a superficial display lacking true spiritual substance. [Sibbes — Works Vol01]

What does the sermon identify as the first way to view the text, and how does it illustrate this with the treatment of the word “saying”?

The sermon explains that the passage may be viewed in a threefold manner, first as “AN ANSWER TO MANY COMPLAINTS.” It illustrates this point by observing that “the word, \"saying,\" is in italics, showing that it is not in the original, but has been supplied by the translators,” and argues that this supplied word has obscured the sense of the original complaint. [Sermon 2880 — "New Tokens of Ancient Love"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2880 — "New Tokens of Ancient Love"]
meta.passage:
It was only on that barren, storm-girt rock, shut out from the world's light, that he could find the fitting darkness in which to view the Glory of Heaven undistracted by the shadows of earth! The message of our text was given to Jeremiah in a time of deep distress-- it was meant to be helpful to the Lord's people in their greatest desolations. That being the case, we may use it in a threefold manner and view it, first, as an answer to many complaints. Secondly, as teaching some exceedingly valuable doc-trinesand, thirdly, as a stimulant to self-examination as to our state before God.

First, then, our text may be viewed as AN ANSWER TO MANY COMPLAINTS.

If you look at your Bibles, you will see that the word, "saying," is in italics, showing that it is not in the original, but has been supplied by the translators. Sometimes they have inserted words which have really brought out the meaning more clearly--but, in this case, if I understand the passage, they have rather obscured the sense. The fact is, the first sentence is a complaint on the part of Israel. In the previous verse, God had said, "The people which were left of the sword found grace in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest." "Ah," said Israel, "but that was centuries ago--'the Lord has appeared of old unto me.'" There was a note of complaint even in the expression of gratitude, as much as to say, "Times are changed, for the Lord does not appear unto me now." The complaint was that His choice Revelations and wondrous deliverances were all in the ages long ago.

What threefold fullness of Christ does Goodwin describe, and how does he connect the church to this fullness?

Goodwin teaches that Christ possesses a personal fullness—the fullness of the Godhead dwelling personally in him—, a dispensatory fullness, in which he "filleth all in all." and from which believers receive grace for grace, and a relative fullness that arises from his relation to the church. He explains that the church is an “empty vessel” that displays his fullness, echoing "My strength is made perfect in weakness." [Goodwin — Works Vol01]

meta.heading: [Goodwin — Works Vol01]
meta.passage:
He mentioneth it, my brethren, as an honour to his church, that she is 
such a body to him, as that though he be a In- id that filleth her, yet he is 
not complete without her. He would shew that Christ needs her not, there- 
fore he saith he filleth her ; he ' filleth aU in all : ' and yet because he is in 
some sense imperfect without her, she is as an ornament to him, therefore he 
addeth she is his fulness ; ' the fulness of him that filleth all in all.' 

Now she is called the fulness of Christ in the same sense that it is said, 
2 Cor. xii. 9, ' My strength is made perfect in weakness.' What, is not 
God's power perfect without our weakness 1 Yes, it is perfect in itself ; but 
it is said to be made perfect, because it is declared to be perfect in weakness. 
So when the church is said to be Christ's fulness, what, is not he full with- 
out her ? Yes, for he ' filleth all in all ;' yet his fulness she is, and she 
setteth off his fulness, because she serveth as an empty vessel for him to fill, 
and to shew his fulness in ; that he is not fuU only in himself personally, but 
that he hath enough overflowing to fill all his body, to fill aU in all. 

Now then to open this, Jesus Christ hath a threefold fulness — 

He hath, first, a personal fulness ; the fulness of the Godhead dwelleth 
personally in him, so Col. ii. 9. 

He hath, secondly, a dispensatory fulness, mentioned here in the text; he 
filleth all in all. ' Of his fulness we all receive grace for grace.' 

Then, thirdly, he hath a relative fulness, which ariseth from a relation to 
his church.

According to Sermon 1429, what biblical passage does Spurgeon cite as the foundation of faith and how does he describe its significance?

Spurgeon teaches that the sure foundation of faith is found in Isaiah 28:16, which he quotes verbatim: "Therefore thus says the Lord God, behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation." He explains that this stone is the object of belief, noting that Paul interprets the promise as "shall not be ashamed" and Peter renders it "shall not be confounded," indicating that believers who trust in this cornerstone will never be disgraced or confused. The repeated citation of this verse by the apostle Paul underscores its central role in establishing a secure basis for Christian faith. [Sermon 1429 — "Faith's Sure Foundation"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 1429 — "Faith's Sure Foundation"]
meta.passage:
We saw the Lord God laying the foundation upon which faith is to rest--we shall now consider the Foundation itself.

The passage before us is a very favorite quotation with the Apostles. If you turn to the Epistle to the Romans you will find Paul quoting it again and again in rapid succession. The last verse of the ninth chapter is, "Whoever believes on Him shall not be ashamed." And in the 11th verse of the 10th chapter he repeats the quotation. It is a quotation from Isaiah 28:16 where we find it written--"Therefore thus says the Lord God, behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation. He that believes shall not make haste," which Paul interprets, "shall not be ashamed" and Peter renders, "shall not be confounded." From the variation of the translations we obtain two or three different shades of meaning but all amounting to the same thing.

That must be a very important part of God's Word which even the Holy Spirit Himself has quoted so frequently! He is prolific of thought and is always able to create new ideas.

What two lessons does Spurgeon say we learn from the seed that falls by the wayside in his sermon "The Seed by the Wayside"?

Spurgeon teaches that believers must recognize that not all efforts bear fruit; he says, "As he sowed, some fell by the wayside; and it was trodden down, and the fowls of the air devoured it," and concludes that we learn two truths: first, we shall have some unprofitable labors, and second, some soils will remain unsuitable for the Good Seed. [Sermon 2843 — "The Seed by the Wayside"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2843 — "The Seed by the Wayside"]
meta.passage:
If you took the end one away, they would all fall down! We want to be self-contained--not merely semi-detached, but altogether detached--so as to be able to stand by ourselves upon our own foundation. God sometimes takes away a helper from us in order that we may learn to lean upon Him, only, and to go about our service in entire dependence upon the Master who is to derive Glory not only from the result of the service, but from the service itself.

It may do us good to talk a little while about our failures. I suppose that we have all had a good many. When some of you began your work for God, you thought that you were going to push the world before you and to drag the Church behind you--but you have not done it yet. You fancied that you were going to convert everybody by your preaching, but, like Melancthon, you have had to say, "Old Adam is too strong for young Melancthon." And you have been driven closer to God by the very failures which you have experienced. If the Holy Spirit shall graciously help us, we may both glorify God and comfort one another while we meditate upon one set of failures with which we are constantly meeting, that is, those that are set forth in these words, "As he sowed, some fell by the wayside; and it was trodden down, and the fowls of the air devoured it."

So, first, we learn that we shall have some unprofitable labors. Secondly, we shall find that some soils will remain unsuitable for the Good Seed.

What does Manton advise a child of God to do regarding worldly possessions and affections?

Manton teaches that a child of God should not be drawn to the fleeting pleasures of the world but should direct his heart toward eternal things. He urges believers to "Set your affections on things above, not on things in the earth," and to subordinate any earthly desire to heavenly priorities, avoiding competition with divine purposes. He also warns against acquiring wealth by unjust means, emphasizing that true happiness lies in the inheritance of God rather than in worldly honor or wealth. [Manton — Works Vol08]

According to Sermon 392, what does the author say is the true source of wisdom and how can it be obtained?

Sermon 392 teaches that true wisdom surpasses all earthly riches—gold, crystal, rubies, topaz— and is obtained solely by trusting in the Lord. The sermon cites, "Whoever trusts in the Lord, happy is he;" as the key statement that connects trust with wise handling of affairs. Thus, according to Spurgeon, the path to wisdom is the simple act of trusting God, which lifts the heaviest burdens and guides one through life's labyrinths. [Sermon 392 — "Trust In God--True Wisdom"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 392 — "Trust In God--True Wisdom"]
meta.passage:
The gold and the crystal cannot equal it--and the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold. No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls--for the price of wisdom is above rubies! The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it--neither shall it be valued with pure gold. From where, then, comes wisdom? And where is the place of understanding, seeing it is hidden from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air? Destruction and Death say, "We have heard the fame thereof with our ears. God understands the way thereof, and He knows the place thereof."

Let us listen, then, to the voice of the Lord, for He has declared the secret; He has revealed to the sons of men wherein true wisdom lies, and we have it in the text, "Whoever trusts in the Lord, happy is he;" and that sentence is put in conjunction with another which teaches us this Truth of God--that to handle a matter wisely is to find good, and the true way to handle a matter wisely is to trust God! This is the short and brief method of escaping the greatest difficulties-- this is the clue to the most intricate labyrinths; this is the lever which shall lift the most tremendous weights. He who trusts in the Lord has found out the way to handle matters wisely, and happy is he!

I shall take the text this morning, by God's assistance, in two ways.

Sibbes explains that the ‘double comfort’ consists of two linked assurances: first, God will raise believers out of present troubles, which he likens to a kind of death, and second, God will raise them out of the grave and present them before the Lord at the final judgment. He writes, "The comfort is double. God will raise us up, and then God will present us with you," indicating that the same power that raised Christ from the dead will also lift the faithful from both temporal afflictions and ultimate death, uniting them forever with Christ. How does Spurgeon describe the emotional significance of the verse "Jesus wept" in his sermon?

Spurgeon teaches that the brief verse "Jesus wept" conveys the depth of Christ’s compassion, portraying a divine heart caught in a great storm of feeling. He says that instead of threatening thunder, the only perceptible sign of the inward tempest was "a shower of tears. For \"Jesus wept.\"" The apostle’s tears are presented as a "blessed shower of tears" that arise from a soul whose "all the forces of His soul were disturbed," yet they produce no judgment, only tender pity. Spurgeon argues that this solitary, sublime verse stands alone as a perfect gem of meaning, impossible to improve by addition, and that if believers expressed righteous indignation in the same compassionate tears, they would fulfill the counsel, "Be you angry and sin not." [Sermon 2091 — "Jesus Wept"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2091 — "Jesus Wept"]
meta.passage:
Between indignation at the powers of evil, grief for the family who had been bereaved by death, sorrow over those who stood by in unbelief and a distressing realization of the effects of sin, the Lord's heart was evidently in a great storm.

Instead of the thunder of threat and the lightning of a curse, all that was perceptible of the inward tempest was a shower of tears. For "Jesus wept." A hurricane rushed through His spirit. All the forces of His soul were disturbed. He shuddered at the sight which was about to be set before Him. He was thrilled from head to foot with emotion. Yet the result of the storm was not a word of terror, nor a glance of judgment but simply a blessed shower of tears--"Jesus wept." If all our righteous indignation displayed itself in tears of pity, we should have fulfilled the text, "Be you angry and sin not."

"Jesus wept." I have often felt vexed with the man, whoever he was, who chopped up the New Testament into verses. He seems to have let the hatchet drop indiscriminately here and there. But I forgive him a great deal of blundering for his wisdom in letting these two words make a verse by themselves--"Jesus wept." This is a diamond of the first water and it cannot have another gem set with it, for it is unique. Shortest of verses in words but where is there a longer one in sense? Add a word to the verse and it would be out of place. No, let it stand in solitary sublimity and simplicity.

meta.passage: Of them he says, Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?' He does not even intend to say that those who were rightly baptized have all of them entered into the fullness of its spiritual meaning; for if they had, there would have been no need of the question, Know ye not?' It would seem that some had been baptized who did not clearly know the meaning of their own baptism. They had faith, and a glimmer of knowledge sufficient to make them right recipients of baptism, but they were not well instructed in the teaching of baptism; perhaps they saw in it only a washing, but had never discerned the burial. I will go further, and say that I question if any of us yet know the fullness of the meaning of either of the ordinances which Christ has instituted. As yet we are, with regard to spiritual things, like children playing on the beach while the ocean rolls before us. At best we wade up to our ankles like our little ones on the sea shore. A few among us are learning to swim; but then we only swim where the bottom is almost within reach. Who among us has yet come to lose sight of shore and to swim in the Atlantic of divine love, where fathomless truth rolls underneath, and the infinite is all around? Oh, may God daily teach us more and more of what we already know in part, and may the truth which we have as yet but dimly perceived come to us in a brighter and clearer manner, till we see all things in clear sunlight.

Why does Manton describe mourning as a holy exercise for Christians?

Manton teaches that mourning serves a sanctifying purpose, stating that "Mourning is a holy exercise, by which the soul is every day more and more weaned from sin, and drawn out to reach after God." He further emphasizes the apostolic instruction that believers should "`Be afflicted, and then `mourn, and then `weep." This continual affliction and sorrow draws the Christian heart toward deeper humility and greater reliance on God, shaping a soul that is increasingly detached from sin and more eager for divine communion. [Manton — Works Vol04]

What does Manton state is the essential condition for believers to obtain heaven under the eternal covenant?

Manton teaches that the covenant between God and Christ grants believers a right to heaven only on the basis of faith, emphasizing that "faith is the solemn condition." He explains that the new birth comes by the infusion of faith and that all hope depends upon this new birth, making faith the decisive requirement for the promised everlasting life. [Manton — Works Vol14]

What does Calvin say about how a Christian should relate to marriage and the use of worldly goods?

Calvin teaches that a believer must adopt a dual discipline: first, "it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none;#8221;" and also treat worldly possessions as if they were not being used, thereby cutting off gluttony, pride, and excess while remaining patient in poverty and moderate in abundance. This balanced approach curbs luxury and prevents the cares of the body from overwhelming the care of the soul. [Calvin — On The Christian Life]

meta.heading: [Calvin — On The Christian Life]
meta.passage:
For
 hence two rules arise: First, "it remaineth, that both they that have
 wives be as though they had none;#8221; "and they that use this world,
 as not abusing it," (1 Cor. vii. 29, 31.) Secondly, we must learn to be
 no less placid and patient in enduring penury, than moderate in
 enjoying abundance. He who makes it his rule to use this world as if he
 used it not, not only cuts off all gluttony in regard to meat and
 drink, and all effeminacy, ambition, pride, excessive shows and
 austerity, in regard to his table, his house, and his clothes, but
 removes every care and affection which might withdraw or hinder him

 soul. [16] It was well said by Cato: Luxury causes great care, and
 produces great carelessness as to virtue; and it is an old
 proverb,--Those who are much occupied with the care of the body,
 usually give little care to the soul. Therefore while the liberty of
 the Christian in external matters is not to be tied down to a strict

 possible; on the other hand, it must be his constant aims not only to
 curb luxury, but to cut off all show of superfluous abundance, and

According to the passage, what is the method of biblical prophecy in handling multiple fulfillments of a single prediction?

The systematic theology author explains that biblical prophecy operates by “predict[ing] the one great end and all else and what preparatory, only so far as it stands in connection with that end and appears as one of its elements.” In this view, a single prophetic utterance can refer to two distinct events, as illustrated by Isaiah’s prediction, which was “so framed as to answer both to the redemption of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon, and to the greater redemption by the Messiah.” Thus the method links the type and its ultimate fulfillment within one prophetic framework. [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol3]

What does Spurgeon mean by the phrase “sweet savor” in his Sermon 688?

Spurgeon teaches that the expression “sweet savor” denotes both the gracious acceptance of God’s people and the acceptance of their worship and service. He explains that believers are received not on their own merit but through Christ, saying, "I will accept you with your sweet savor," and that this acceptance extends to their offerings, prayers, and praises once they are reconciled to Him. Thus, the sweet savor signifies the pleasing fragrance of a redeemed heart and its devoted deeds before a merciful Father. [Sermon 688 — "Sweet Savor"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 688 — "Sweet Savor"]
meta.passage:
They had so thoroughly defiled themselves, and after so many trials had been so desperately incorrigible, that one would have supposed the chapter would have concluded with thunderbolts of vengeance and a terrible voice condemning them to be driven forever from the face of the Most High. Instead of this it concludes with mercy! The trumpet ceases its loud swell, and the melodious tone of the harp is heard in gentle notes of melody. The thunder and the lightning are over, the storm is past, and the still small voice, in refreshing calm, proclaims the infinite pardon that proceeds from a tender Father's heart.

Our text seems to me very full of fatness. Its savor will be doubtless passing sweet to those who have grace to appreciate it. We shall contemplate it in two lights. First we have a promise that the persons of His people shall be accepted as a sweet savor. Sinners are accepted through the merits of Christ: "I will accept you with your sweet savor." I cannot accept you otherwise, but I will accept you thus. Then, secondly (which is more consistent with the context), we are assured that our offerings shall be accepted--"I will accept you with your sweet savor." I will not only love and receive you, but I will also receive your worship and your service.

Your sweet savor, those same things which once you offered to idols, you shall from now on bring as an offering to Me and when I have accepted you and you are reconciled to Me, then I will accept your good works and your prayers, and your praises, too.

' I.

According to Spurgeon in this sermon, what should be the proper motive and attitude of Christians toward prayer?

Spurgeon teaches that prayer ought to be embraced as a delightful, cherished element of the Christian life rather than merely a compulsory duty. He urges believers to regard it as "one of heaven's best luxuries" and to esteem it "more than your necessary food," seeking to move from a low state of grace to a higher, healthier atmosphere of devotion. He also stresses that prayer should be directed toward definite requests, noting that the Savior spoke of "what things soever ye desire," indicating that believers should have specific objects of petition. Spurgeon therefore calls Christians to look at the text, look about them, and look above, cultivating a love for prayer that springs from desire rather than obligation. [Sermon 328 — "True Prayer—True Power!"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 328 — "True Prayer—True Power!"]
meta.passage:
There are many Christians, I think, who have to complain of this—that they pray not so much because it is a blessed thing to allowed to draw near to God, as because they must pray, because it is their duty, because they feel that if they did not, they would lose one of the sure evidences of being Christians. Brethren, I do not condemn you; but at the same time, if I may be the means of lifting you up this morning from so low a state of grace into a higher and more healthy atmosphere, my soul shall be exceeding glad. If I can show you a more excellent way; if from this time forth you may come to look at prayer as your element, as one of the most delightful exercises of your life; if you shall come to esteem it more than your necessary food, and to value it as one of heaven's best luxuries, surely I shall have answered a great end, and you shall have to thank God for a great blessing.

Give me than your attention while I beg you, first, to look at the text; secondly to look about you; and the, to look above you.

First, LOOK AT THE TEXT. If you look at it carefully, I think you will perceive the essential qualities which are necessary to any great success and prevalence in prayer. According to our Saviour's description of prayer, there should always be some definite objects for which we should plead. He speaks of things—"what things soever ye desire." It seems then that he did not put it that God's children would go to him to pray when they have nothing to pray for.
